situation: You're at an airport check-in desk, about to fly to Berlin with one suitcase.

options: Sure, here you go.
Sure, take it from me.
Sure, this is for you.
Sure, I give it to you.
turns.answer: Sure, here you go.
turns.why: "Here you go" is the natural phrase when you hand something to someone.

turns.line: Agent: Thanks. Are you checking any bags today?

Only this. The others I take with me.
Just this one. I have more in hand.
Only this one. Others are on me.
turns.answer: Just this one. The rest is carry-on.

I prefer to sit near of window.
Window, I want it very much.
To sit by window is better for me.

situation: You're in a hotel room in New York and the air conditioning isn't working.

Hi, the AC in my room isn't work.
Hi, my room has a problem with AC not work.
Hi, the AC at my room is not functioning.

That is good, I will wait you.
Okay, I am waiting him now.
It's fine, send him until ten minutes.
turns.answer: That would be great, thanks.
turns.why: It's the natural, polite way to accept an offer. We say "wait for", not "wait you".

situation: You're in Rome and you're lost, looking for the train station.

Yes, please. Where is the way to train station?
Yes, please. I need that you show me the station.
Yes, please. Tell me how I go to the station.
turns.answer: Yes, please. How do I get to the train station?
turns.why: "How do I get to...?" is the standard way to ask for directions.

Got it. Is it long from here?
Got it. How much it is from here?
Got it. It is a lot of distance?
turns.answer: Got it. Is it far from here?
turns.why: We use "far" for distance. "Long" is for time, so it doesn't fit here.

situation: You're at a car rental counter in Los Angeles.

turns.line: Clerk: Hi! What kind of car are you looking for?

I want a car that is little and not expensive.
Give me the most cheap and small one.
A small car, because I am without much money.
turns.answer: Something small and cheap would be fine.

During four days, to Sunday.
Since four days, until the Sunday.
Four days long, up to Sunday.

turns.line: Clerk: Perfect. Do you want to add full insurance?
options: What does it cover exactly?
What it is covering exactly?
What does it covers exactly?
What does that cover it exactly?
turns.answer: What does it cover exactly?
turns.why: Questions need "does" before the subject, and the verb stays simple: "cover".

situation: You're on a train in England and someone is sitting in your reserved seat.

turns.line: Passenger: Oh, is this your seat? Sorry!
options: No worries, I think it's seat 14B.
No worries, I think this is mine seat.
No worry, my seat is the one you sit.
No problem, you need to go from here.

turns.line: Passenger: Let me check my ticket. Oh, I'm in the wrong carriage!

Don't worry, it is happening every time.
Don't worry, this is happen a lot of times.
Don't worry, it was happening always.

turns.why: Use the present simple for things that happen often: "it happens all the time".

situation: You're checking out of a hotel in Sydney and looking at your bill.

turns.line: Receptionist: Here's your bill. Did you enjoy your stay?
options: Yes, it was great. The staff were very helpful.
Yes, it was great. The staff was very helping.
Yes, it is great. The staff were very help.
Yes, it was great. The staffs were helpful.
turns.answer: Yes, it was great. The staff were very helpful.
turns.why: Use the past tense for a finished stay. "Staff" has no "s", and "helpful" is the right word.

turns.line: Receptionist: Wonderful. Is everything on the bill correct?
options: Actually, I think I was charged twice for the minibar.
Actually, I think you charged me two times the minibar.
Actually, I think the minibar is paid by me twice.
Actually, I think I was charge twice for minibar.
turns.answer: Actually, I think I was charged twice for the minibar.

Thanks a lot, I appreciate from you.
Thank you, I am very appreciating this.
Thanks, I appreciate it you very much.
turns.answer: Thanks a lot, I really appreciate it.
turns.why: "I appreciate it" is the natural phrase. "Appreciate" is not used in continuous form here.

situation: You're at a hostel in Amsterdam, asking about the shared kitchen.

Yeah, there is a kitchen that I can to use?
Yeah, have you a kitchen for use of me?
Yeah, is existing a kitchen to cook?

Great. Need I to bring my pots myself?
Great. I must to bring pots from me?
Great. Do I need bring own pots?
turns.answer: Great. Do I need to bring my own pots?
turns.why: After "need" we use "to" plus the verb: "need to bring". "Do I...?" makes it a question.

situation: You're at an airport gate in Tokyo and your flight has just been delayed.

Excuse me, you know why is the delay?
Excuse me, what is the reason the delay is?
Excuse me, tell me why you delayed it.

turns.why: "Do you know...?" is polite, and the word order stays normal after "what".

turns.line: Gate agent: It's just bad weather. We'll update you soon.
options: Okay. Will we get a food voucher?
Okay. We will receive a voucher of food?
Okay. Are we getting voucher for eat?
Okay. It will be a voucher to us?

Perfect, I go there from now.
Perfect, I am going there since now.
Perfect, I will to go there now.

turns.why: "I'll" is a natural way to say a decision made at the moment of speaking.

situation: You're at the front desk of your hotel in Chicago, and you want to book a tour for tomorrow.

Hi, I am wanting to booking a city tour.

turns.line: Concierge: Sure! We have one at nine and one at two. Which one works better for you?

The morning one is more better for me.
I think the morning is the more good.
The morning, it is more comfortable to me.

turns.why: "Works better" is the natural way to say a time suits you more.

situation: You're at the front desk of a hotel in London, checking in after a long flight.

turns.line: Receptionist: Good evening! Welcome. Do you have a reservation with us?
options: Yes, I booked a room under the name Daniel Katz.
Yes, I have ordered a room on the name Daniel Katz.
Yes, I booked one room at the name Daniel Katz.
Yes, I am reserving a room by the name Daniel Katz.
turns.answer: Yes, I booked a room under the name Daniel Katz.
turns.why: We say a booking is "under" a name, and the past tense "booked" fits something you already did.

turns.line: Receptionist: Perfect, I found it. It's for three nights, right? Would you like a room on a high floor?
options: Yes, please. Somewhere quiet would be great, if possible.
Yes, please. I want that you give me a quiet room.
Yes, please. Somewhere quiet would be great, if it's possibly.
Yes, please. I would like quiet room, if you can to do it.
turns.answer: Yes, please. Somewhere quiet would be great, if possible.
turns.why: "If possible" is the natural polite phrase. The others use wrong forms like "want that you give", "if it's possibly" or leave out "a".

situation: You're at the airport, and the agent at the check-in counter is looking at your bag.

turns.line: Agent: Hi there. Is this your only bag, or do you have more to check in?
options: Just this one. It's my only bag.
Only this one. I don't have more of them bags.
Just this one. There is not other one by me.
Just this one. I have not another.
turns.answer: Just this one. It's my only bag.
turns.why: Short, clear and natural. The other options use wrong grammar or translate word for word.

turns.line: Agent: Great. Could you put it on the scale, please? Hmm, it's a little over the limit.
options: Oh no, sorry! Can I take something out and put it in my backpack?
Oh no, sorry! Can I take out something and to put it in my backpack?
Oh no, sorry! Can I to take something out and put him in my backpack?
Oh no, sorry! Can I take something out and put in my backpack it?
turns.answer: Oh no, sorry! Can I take something out and put it in my backpack?
turns.why: After "can" we use the plain verb, and "it" goes before "in my backpack".

turns.line: Agent: Sure, go ahead. Just move a few things over and we'll weigh it again.

Thanks, that should to do it. I will be quick.
Thanks, this is should do it. I'm being quick.
Thanks, that should doing it. I be quick.
turns.answer: Thanks, that should do it. I'll be quick.
turns.why: "Should" is followed by the plain verb, and "I'll be quick" is the natural way to promise speed.

situation: You're in a hotel room in Boston and the shower has no hot water.

turns.line: Receptionist: Front desk, how can I help you?
options: Hi, there's no hot water in my shower. Could you send someone to check it?
Hi, in my shower there isn't hot water. You must to send someone now.
Hi, the water in the shower is not hot, so fix it immediately.
Hi, my shower doesn't has hot water. Send somebody here at once.
turns.answer: Hi, there's no hot water in my shower. Could you send someone to check it?
turns.why: It states the problem clearly and asks politely. The others are too blunt or have grammar mistakes.

turns.line: Receptionist: I'm so sorry about that. Someone can come up in about ten minutes. Is that okay?
options: Yes, that's fine. I'll be in the room until then.
Yes, that's fine. I will be at the room until it.
Yes, that's fine. I stay in the room until then.
Yes, that's fine. I'm being in room until then.
turns.answer: Yes, that's fine. I'll be in the room until then.
turns.why: "I'll be" is the natural way to promise something about the near future, and "until then" fits the time.

situation: You're on a train in the UK and you're not sure if you're in the right seat.

turns.line: Passenger: Excuse me, I think you're sitting in my seat. I booked this one.
options: Oh, really? Sorry, let me check my ticket.
Oh, really? Sorry, I will look on my ticket now.
Oh, really? Sorry, let me to check my ticket.
Oh, really? Sorry, I am checking from my ticket.
turns.answer: Oh, really? Sorry, let me check my ticket.
turns.why: "Let me" is followed by the plain verb, which makes it a natural, polite response.

turns.line: Passenger: No problem. What does your ticket say?
options: It says coach C, seat 14. Is this seat 14?
It says coach C, seat 14. This is the seat 14?
It's saying coach C, seat 14. Is this seat 14?
It says coach C, seat 14. Is it the seat 14 here?
turns.answer: It says coach C, seat 14. Is this seat 14?
turns.why: We say seat numbers without "the", and "it says" is the normal way to read a ticket.

turns.line: Passenger: Ah, this is seat 41. Yours is two rows back, I think.
options: Oh, my mistake! Thanks for letting me know.
Oh, my mistake! Thanks that you told me.
Oh, my mistake! Thanks for tell me this.
Oh, my mistake! Thank you for you let me know.
turns.answer: Oh, my mistake! Thanks for letting me know.
turns.why: After "thanks for" we use the "-ing" form, so "letting me know" is correct.

situation: You're at a hotel in New York and you want to leave your bags after check-out.

turns.line: Receptionist: Good morning! Did you enjoy your stay?
options: Yes, it was great. Thanks! I'd like to check out now.
Yes, it was great. Thanks! I want to do check out now.
Yes, it was great. Thanks! I will to check out right now.
Yes, it was great. Thanks! I like check out now.
turns.answer: Yes, it was great. Thanks! I'd like to check out now.
turns.why: "I'd like to" is the polite way to say what you want to do.

turns.line: Receptionist: No problem. Here's your bill. Is there anything else I can help with?
options: Yes, could I leave my bags here until the evening?
Yes, can I leave my bags in here until in the evening?
Yes, I can to leave my bags here till the evening?
Yes, may I leaving my bags here until evening time?
turns.answer: Yes, could I leave my bags here until the evening?
turns.why: "Could I" is a polite request followed by the plain verb, and "until the evening" is the natural phrase.

situation: You're in Dublin and you stop a local on the street to ask how to get to the train station.

turns.line: Local: Sure, no problem! Where are you trying to go?
options: I'm trying to get to the train station. Is it far from here?
I try to arrive to the train station. It is far from here?
I'm trying to arrive at the train station. Is far from here?
I want go to the train station. It's far by here?
turns.answer: I'm trying to get to the train station. Is it far from here?
turns.why: "Get to" is the natural way to say reaching a place, and the question needs "is it" in that order.

Got it, straight and after that left in the bank. Thanks a lot!
Got it, I go straight and I turn left on the bank. Thanks!
Got it, straight and then to left at the bank. Thank you much!
turns.answer: Got it, straight and then left at the bank. Thanks a lot!
turns.why: We turn left "at" a landmark, and "Thanks a lot" is the natural phrase.

situation: You're at a car rental desk in Los Angeles and you want to pick up the car you booked online.

turns.answer: Hi, I'm here to pick up a car I reserved online.
turns.why: "Pick up" is the natural phrase for collecting a rental car, and "online" needs no "in" or "on".

Sure, here you are. Must I to pay something now?
Sure, take it. I need pay something right now?
Sure, here it is. Am I needing to pay something now?
turns.answer: Sure, here you go. Do I need to pay anything now?
turns.why: "Here you go" is what we say when handing something over, and "Do I need to" is the normal question form.

turns.line: Agent: No, you're all set. Just bring it back with a full tank, please.

No problem. I fill it up before I will return it.
No problem. I'll fill it before that I return him.
No problem. I will to fill up it before returning.
turns.answer: No problem. I'll fill it up before I return it.
turns.why: After "before" we use the present tense, even for the future, so "before I return it" is correct.

situation: You're on a plane to Rome and the flight attendant comes by with the drinks cart.

turns.why: "Could I have" is a polite and natural way to ask for something.

I'm okay, thanks. I ate already before that I came to the plane.
I'm okay, thanks. I have eaten before I am getting on plane.
I'm okay, thanks. I was eating already before the plane.
turns.answer: I'm okay, thanks. I already ate before I got on the plane.
turns.why: Use the past tense for both actions. "Got on the plane" is the natural phrase.

situation: You're at a hotel breakfast in Sydney and you're talking to the waiter about your room.

turns.line: Waiter: Good morning! What's your room number?
options: It's room 312. I'm staying here until Friday.
It's the room 312. I stay here to Friday.
It's room 312. I'm stay here until the Friday.
It is room 312. I am staying here since Friday.
turns.answer: It's room 312. I'm staying here until Friday.
turns.why: We say room numbers without "the", and "until" shows when something ends.

turns.line: Waiter: Thanks! Would you like tea or coffee?

Coffee, please. I can also take more of toast?
Coffee, please. Also I am wanting more toasts.
Coffee, please. Can I get also some toast more?
turns.answer: Coffee, please. Can I also get some more toast?
turns.why: "Toast" is not counted, so we say "some more toast", and "also" goes before the verb "get".

turns.line: Waiter: Sure thing. I'll bring it out in a few minutes.

Great, thank you. I don't have a rush.
Great, thank you. I'm not in hurry.
Great, thank you. I have no any rush.
turns.answer: Great, thank you. I'm in no rush.
turns.why: "I'm in no rush" is a common, natural way to say you can wait.

situation: You're at a train station in Berlin and you want to buy a ticket to the airport.

Hi, I want that you give me ticket for airport.
Hi, give me a ticket to the airport now.
Hi, I'm needing one ticket at the airport.
turns.answer: Hi, I'd like a ticket to the airport, please.
turns.why: "I'd like" is polite and natural. The others are too blunt or use wrong grammar.

turns.line: Clerk: Sure. One way or return?

Just one way, please. How much it costs?
Just one way, please. What is the cost it?
Just one way, please. How many is it?
turns.answer: Just one way, please. How much is it?
turns.why: "How much is it?" is the correct question form for asking a price.

Perfect, thanks. I hurry so I not miss it.
Perfect, thanks. I'll hurry for don't miss him.
Perfect, thanks. I will hurrying that I don't miss.
turns.answer: Perfect, thanks. I'll hurry so I don't miss it.

situation: You're at the bus stop and run into a neighbor you haven't seen for a while.

Pretty good, thanks. I just busy with work lately.
Pretty good, thanks. I have a lot of work on me.
Pretty good. What do you care? I've been busy.
turns.answer: Pretty good, thanks. I've just been busy with work.
turns.why: "I've been busy" (present perfect) is the natural way to describe a period up to now. The others are broken or rude.

turns.line: Neighbor: Same here. Are you still living on Maple Street?

Yes, I live there since six years now.
Yes, I'm living there from six years now.
Yes, I lived there for six years now.
turns.answer: Yes, I've lived there for six years now.
turns.why: For something that started in the past and still continues, use the present perfect with "for" and a length of time.

situation: You're getting coffee when a coworker stops to chat on Monday morning.

It was great, thanks. We have been to the beach on Saturday.
It was great, thanks. We went to the beach in Saturday.
turns.answer: It was great, thanks. We went to the beach on Saturday.
turns.why: Use the past simple for a finished time, and "on" with days of the week.

Not really. Was pretty quiet for July.
Not really. It was a few people only.
Not really. Why do you even ask that?
turns.answer: Not really. It was pretty quiet for July.
turns.why: English sentences need a subject like "it". "Why do you even ask that?" is rude for friendly small talk.

situation: You're in an elevator with a stranger on a rainy afternoon.

I know! It's raining from buckets outside.
Why are you talking to me about it?
turns.answer: I know! It was sunny an hour ago.
turns.why: It's a friendly, natural reply with the right past tense. "Raining from buckets" is a word-for-word Hebrew idiom.

Bye! Finally, I can stop talking.

turns.why: "You too" is the normal short reply to "Have a good one", and "out there" is the natural phrase.

situation: You're at a friend's party and a guy you've never met starts talking to you.

We were working together before two years.

turns.why: "Used to" describes something that was true in the past but isn't anymore. The other options are wrong grammar or rude.

turns.line: Dan: Oh nice. I'm her cousin, actually. I just moved here from Boston.

Oh wow, welcome! How you like it so far?
Oh wow, welcome! How do you liking it so far?
Oh wow, welcome! How it is liking you so far?
turns.answer: Oh wow, welcome! How are you liking it so far?
turns.why: Questions need the helper word in the right place: "How are you liking...". The others have the wrong word order.

turns.line: Dan: It's great, but I don't know many people yet.

Well, you can come hang out with we sometime.
Well, you can come hanging out with us sometime.
Well, you can to come hang out with us sometime.
turns.answer: Well, you can come hang out with us sometime.
turns.why: After "with" use "us", and after "can" use the plain verb with no "to".

situation: You're in a taxi after a long day and the driver starts chatting.

Yeah, I don't sleep much last night.

Not really. I just go relax at the home.
Not really. I will relaxing at the home.
turns.answer: Not really. I'm just going to relax at home.
turns.why: We say "at home" with no "the", and "going to" is the natural way to talk about plans.

Hi, I'm Noa. Nice to know you.

Hi, I am Noa. Why do you ask?
turns.answer: Hi, I'm Noa. Nice to meet you.

turns.line: Mum: Lovely! Are you in the same class as Tom?
options: Yes, we sit next to each other in maths.
Yes, we sit one near the other in maths.
Yes, we are sitting next to us in maths.
Yes, we sitted next to each other in maths.
turns.answer: Yes, we sit next to each other in maths.
turns.why: "Next to each other" is the natural phrase. "Sitted" isn't a word. The past of "sit" is "sat".

turns.line: Mum: That's nice. Anyway, I'd better go. My bus is coming!
options: Of course! It was nice meeting you.
Of course! It was nice to know you.
Of course! Nice to meeting you.
Of course! Go, go, I'm bored anyway.
turns.answer: Of course! It was nice meeting you.
turns.why: When saying goodbye, "nice meeting you" is the natural phrase. The last option is rude.

situation: You're at the gym and a guy on the next machine starts talking to you.

turns.line: Guy: You come here a lot, right? I think I've seen you before.
options: Yeah, I usually come here after work.
Yeah, I use to come here after work.
Yeah, I usually come to here after work.
Yeah, I am used to come here after work.
turns.answer: Yeah, I usually come here after work.
turns.why: "Usually" plus the present simple describes a habit. "Here" already means "to this place", so no "to" is needed.

turns.line: Guy: Cool. I'm Jake, by the way. Do you have a favorite machine?
options: Honestly, I like the bike best. It's relaxing.
Honestly, I like more the bike. It's relaxing.
Honestly, I like the bike best. He is relaxing.
Honestly, I like the bike best. It's relax.
turns.answer: Honestly, I like the bike best. It's relaxing.
turns.why: Use "it" for things, not "he". "Relax" is a verb. To describe something, say "relaxing".

situation: You're in the office kitchen on your first day back from a trip to Italy.

turns.line: Coworker: Hey, you're back! How was your trip to Italy?
options: It was amazing. I'd love to go back.
It was amazing. I would love to went back.
It was amazing. I love to returning there.
It was amazing. I want that I will go back.
turns.answer: It was amazing. I'd love to go back.
turns.why: After "would love to" use the plain verb. The others mix up verb forms or copy Hebrew sentence structure.

turns.line: Coworker: Did you try the food? I've heard it's incredible.
options: Yes! I had the best pizza of my life.
Yes! I ate the best pizza from my life.
Yes! I had the most best pizza ever.
Yes! I have eaten the best pizza yesterday.
turns.answer: Yes! I had the best pizza of my life.
turns.why: We say "the best ... of my life". "Most best" is double, and the present perfect can't go with "yesterday".

turns.line: Coworker: Ha, jealous! Anyway, welcome back. Catch up soon?
options: Definitely! Let's grab lunch one day this week.
Definitely! Let's to grab lunch one day this week.
Definitely! Let's grabbing lunch one day this week.
Definitely! Let's grab lunch one day on this week.
turns.answer: Definitely! Let's grab lunch one day this week.
turns.why: After "let's" use the plain verb, and "this week" needs no preposition.

situation: You're at a café in Tel Aviv and a tourist at the next table starts a conversation.

turns.line: Tourist: Hi! Do you live here, or are you visiting too?
options: I live here. I was born in Haifa.
I live here. I am born in Haifa.
I live here. I born in Haifa.
I live here. I was born at Haifa.
turns.answer: I live here. I was born in Haifa.
turns.why: "Born" always goes with "was" in the past, and we say "in" with a city.

turns.line: Tourist: Lucky you! Can you recommend a good place for dinner?
options: Sure! There's a great little place around the corner.
Sure! Is a great little place around the corner.
Sure! It exists a great little place around the corner.
Sure! Find it yourself, I'm busy right now.
turns.answer: Sure! There's a great little place around the corner.
turns.why: To say something exists somewhere, start with "There's". The last option is rude to a friendly question.

situation: A friend you haven't spoken to for months calls you.

turns.line: Friend: Hey, stranger! I haven't heard from you in ages.
options: I know, I'm sorry. Things have been crazy lately.
I know, I'm sorry. Things were crazy lately.
I know, I'm sorry. Things are being crazy since weeks.
I know. It's your fault, you never called me.
turns.answer: I know, I'm sorry. Things have been crazy lately.
turns.why: "Lately" goes with the present perfect ("have been"). Blaming your friend is too blunt here.

turns.line: Friend: No worries! So what's new? Anything exciting?
options: Actually, yes! I just got a new job.
Actually, yes! I just get a new job.
Actually, yes! I'm just got a new job.
Actually, yes! I have got a new job yesterday.
turns.answer: Actually, yes! I just got a new job.
turns.why: "Just" with a finished recent event takes the past simple: "just got".

turns.line: Friend: No way, congrats! Where are you working now?
options: It's a small design company downtown. I start on Monday.
It's a small design company downtown. I start at Monday.
It's a small design company downtown. I starting on Monday.
It's a small design company downtown. I started on next Monday.
turns.answer: It's a small design company downtown. I start on Monday.
turns.why: Use "on" with days. The present simple works for a fixed future plan like a start date.

situation: You're at a coffee shop and you run into a neighbour you haven't seen in a while.

turns.line: Neighbour: Hey! Long time no see. How've you been?
options: Pretty good, thanks. Just busy with work. You?
I am being good, thanks. Busy with the work. You?
Pretty good, thanks. Just busy with work. And you are?
I was good, thanks. Just busy with work. How you?
turns.answer: Pretty good, thanks. Just busy with work. You?
turns.why: This is a natural, short reply that returns the question. The others have wrong tense or word order, or ask a different question.

turns.line: Neighbour: Same here. We should grab a coffee sometime!
options: Definitely! Let's text and pick a day.
Definitely! I will to text you and pick day.
Definitely! Let's to text and pick a day.
Definitely! We text and we pick a day.
turns.answer: Definitely! Let's text and pick a day.
turns.why: "Let's" is followed by the base verb, with no "to".

situation: You're at a bus stop and a stranger starts chatting about the weather.

turns.line: Stranger: Wow, it's so hot today, isn't it?
options: Yeah, it's crazy. I can't wait for autumn.
Yeah, it makes hot. I can't wait for autumn.
Yeah, it's crazy. I can't wait to the autumn.
Yeah, is crazy. I can't wait for autumn.
turns.answer: Yeah, it's crazy. I can't wait for autumn.
turns.why: "It's" is needed as the subject, and "wait for" is the right phrase with a noun.

turns.line: Stranger: Tell me about it. I'm melting out here.
options: Same. I hope the bus comes soon.
Same. I hoping the bus comes soon.
Same. I hope the bus is coming soon he.
Same. I hope that bus come soon.
turns.answer: Same. I hope the bus comes soon.
turns.why: We say "I hope", not "I hoping". "The bus" is one thing, so the verb is "comes".

situation: You're at a friend's birthday party and you meet someone new.

turns.line: Dana: Hi, I'm Dana. How do you know Noam?
options: We work together. We started in the same week.
We are working together. We started in same week.
We work together. We are starting in the same week.
We work together. We started at the same week.
turns.answer: We work together. We started in the same week.
turns.why: We say "in the same week" for a time period, and the past tense for something that already happened.

turns.line: Dana: Oh nice! What do you do?
options: I'm a designer. What about you?
I work like a designer. What about you?
I'm designer. What about you?
I do a designer. What about you?
turns.answer: I'm a designer. What about you?
turns.why: We say "I'm a" plus the job. "Work like" and "do" sound wrong here.

turns.line: Dana: I'm a teacher. I teach middle school.
options: That sounds tough! Do you like it?
That sounds tough! You are liking it?
That sounds tough! Do you like this?
That sounds tough! Like you it?
turns.answer: That sounds tough! Do you like it?
turns.why: Questions with "like" use "Do you like it?" and not a statement with "are liking".

situation: You're in the office kitchen on Monday morning, chatting with a coworker.

turns.line: Coworker: Morning! Did you have a good weekend?
options: Yeah, it was great. We went to the beach.
Yeah, it was great. We go to the beach.
Yeah, it was great. We were go to the beach.
Yeah, it was great. We went in the beach.
turns.answer: Yeah, it was great. We went to the beach.
turns.why: The weekend is over, so use the past tense "went", and say "to the beach".

turns.line: Coworker: Nice! I just stayed home and relaxed.
options: That sounds good too. I needed a rest myself.
That sounds good too. I needed rest by myself.
That sounds good too. I need a rest myself yesterday.
That sounds good too. I was needing a rest myself.
turns.answer: That sounds good too. I needed a rest myself.
turns.why: "Myself" is natural here, and "needed" is the simple past for a finished time.

situation: You're waiting for a movie to start and the person next to you says hello.

turns.line: Man: Have you seen this movie before?
options: No, this is my first time. Is it good?
No, I didn't see it before. It is good?
No, this is my first time. It is good?
No, I never see it before. Is it good?
turns.answer: No, this is my first time. Is it good?
turns.why: "This is my first time" is natural, and questions put "is" before "it".

turns.line: Man: I've seen it twice. It's really funny.
options: Awesome! I can't wait to see it.
Awesome! I can't wait for see it.
Awesome! I don't wait to see it.
Awesome! I can't wait seeing it.
turns.answer: Awesome! I can't wait to see it.
turns.why: "Can't wait" is followed by "to" and the base verb.

situation: You're at the gym and someone you see often says hi.

turns.line: Gym buddy: Hey, you're here early today!
options: Yeah, I couldn't sleep, so I came in.
Yeah, I couldn't to sleep, so I came in.

Yeah, I didn't could sleep, so I came in.
turns.answer: Yeah, I couldn't sleep, so I came in.
turns.why: "Couldn't" is the past of "can't", and it is followed by the base verb.

turns.line: Gym buddy: Ugh, I hate when that happens. Want to work out together?
options: Sure, why not? I'll go first on the bench.
Sure, why not? I go first on the bench.
Sure, why not? I'm going first to the bench.
Sure, why not? I will to go first on the bench.
turns.answer: Sure, why not? I'll go first on the bench.
turns.why: "I'll" is natural for a decision made right now.

turns.line: Gym buddy: Cool. How long have you been coming here?
options: About a year now. I really like it.
From a year now. I really like it.
Since a year now. I really like it.
About a year ago. I really like it.
turns.answer: About a year now. I really like it.
turns.why: "About a year" shows how long. "From" and "since" don't work with a length of time.

situation: You're on a flight and the passenger next to you wants to talk.

turns.line: Passenger: Are you going on vacation or is this for work?
options: Vacation! I'm visiting my sister in London.
Vacation! I visit my sister in London.
Vacation! I'm visiting to my sister in London.
Vacation! I will visiting my sister in London.
turns.answer: Vacation! I'm visiting my sister in London.
turns.why: We use the present continuous for a plan that is already arranged, and "visit" has no "to".

turns.line: Passenger: Lovely! Is it your first time there?
options: No, I've been there a few times.
No, I've went there a few times.
No, I am there a few times.
No, I have been there since few times.
turns.answer: No, I've been there a few times.
turns.why: The present perfect ("I've been") is for experiences up to now. "I've went" is wrong because "went" can't follow "have".

situation: You're at a family dinner and your friend's mom asks about you.

turns.line: Mrs. Cohen: So, how's school going?
options: It's going well. I have a big test next week.
It goes well. I have a big test next week.
It's going well. I have a big test in next week.
It's going well. I am have a big test next week.
turns.answer: It's going well. I have a big test next week.
turns.why: "How's it going" is answered with "It's going well". We say "I have a test", and "next week" needs no preposition.

turns.line: Mrs. Cohen: Good luck! Are you studying a lot?
options: Yeah, every night. I hope I pass.
Yeah, every night. I hope I passing.
Yeah, all the night. I hope I pass.
Yeah, every night. I hope to I pass.
turns.answer: Yeah, every night. I hope I pass.
turns.why: "Every night" means each night. After "I hope I" we use a normal verb like "pass", not "passing".

situation: You're at a pool party and a friend of a friend sits down beside you.

turns.line: Tom: Hi! I don't think we've met. I'm Tom.
options: Nice to meet you, Tom. I'm Yael.
Nice to know you, Tom. I'm Yael.
Nice to meet you, Tom. My name Yael.
Nice to meet you, Tom. I call Yael.
turns.answer: Nice to meet you, Tom. I'm Yael.
turns.why: When we meet someone for the first time, we say "Nice to meet you", not "Nice to know you".

turns.line: Tom: So, are you from around here?
options: Yeah, I grew up a few blocks away.
Yeah, I grow up a few blocks away.
Yeah, I grew up few blocks away.
Yeah, I was grown up a few blocks away.
turns.answer: Yeah, I grew up a few blocks away.
turns.why: "Grew up" is the past tense for childhood, and we say "a few" before a plural noun.

turns.line: Tom: Cool. This is a great spot for a party.
options: Totally. The music is really good too.
Totally. The music it is really good too.
Totally. The music are really good too.
Totally. The music is very much good too.
turns.answer: Totally. The music is really good too.
turns.why: "Music" is a single thing, so we use "is", and "really good" sounds natural.

situation: You're at school pickup and another parent starts a chat.

turns.line: Parent: Hi! Your daughter and mine are in the same class, right?
options: Yes, they're good friends. They play every day.
Yes, they are good friends. They plays every day.
Yes, they're good friends. They play in every day.
Yes, they're good friend. They play every day.
turns.answer: Yes, they're good friends. They play every day.
turns.why: With "they" we say "play", not "plays". "Friends" must be plural after "they're".

turns.line: Parent: That's so sweet. Maybe we can set up a playdate.
options: I'd love that. Is Saturday good for you?
I'd love that. Saturday is good by you?
I'd love that. It's Saturday good for you?
I'd love that. Is Saturday good to you?
turns.answer: I'd love that. Is Saturday good for you?
turns.why: We ask "Is Saturday good for you?" to check if a day works for someone.

situation: You're at a coffee shop and a stranger next to you smiles at your laptop sticker.

turns.line: Stranger: Nice sticker! Are you a big fan of that band?
options: Yeah, I've been listening to them since high school.
Yeah, I listen to them from high school.
Yeah, I am listening to them since high school.
Yeah, I was listening to them since high school.
turns.answer: Yeah, I've been listening to them since high school.
turns.why: Use the present perfect continuous (have been listening) with 'since' for something that started in the past and still continues.

turns.line: Stranger: Cool! Have you ever seen them live?
options: Not yet, but I'd love to.
Not yet, but I'd love.
Not yet, but I would love it to.
Not yet, but I loved to.

turns.why: 'I'd love to' is the natural short way to say you really want to do something. Don't drop the 'to'.

situation: You're in the office kitchen on Monday morning and a coworker walks in.

turns.line: Coworker: Morning! How was your weekend?
options: Pretty good, thanks. We just relaxed at home.
Pretty good, thanks. We just made relax at home.
Pretty good, thanks. We just relaxing at home.
Pretty good, thanks. We just relaxed in the home.
turns.answer: Pretty good, thanks. We just relaxed at home.
turns.why: Use the past tense for a finished weekend, and say 'at home' without 'the'.

turns.line: Coworker: Nice. Did you do anything fun?
options: Not really, we watched a few movies.
Not really, we saw a few movies in the TV.
Not really, we are watching a few movies.
Not really, we have watched a few movies yesterday.
turns.answer: Not really, we watched a few movies.
turns.why: Use the simple past for finished actions. Present perfect doesn't go with a time like 'yesterday'.

turns.line: Coworker: Sounds perfect. I'm still looking for something good to watch this week.
options: Ha, same here. Let me know if you find any good movies!
Ha, same here. Tell me if you will find any good movies!
Ha, same here. Let me know if you will find good movies!
Ha, same here. Say me if you find any good movies!
turns.answer: Ha, same here. Let me know if you find any good movies!
turns.why: After 'if', use the present tense for future ideas, and say 'let me know', not 'say me'.

situation: You're waiting for a bus and an older woman next to you starts chatting about the weather.

turns.line: Woman: It's freezing today, isn't it?
options: It really is. I wish I'd brought a warmer coat.
It really is. I wish I brought a more warm coat.
It really is. I wish I will bring a warmer coat.
It really is. I wish I have brought warm coat.
turns.answer: It really is. I wish I'd brought a warmer coat.
turns.why: To talk about a past regret, use 'I wish I had' plus the past participle, like 'I wish I'd brought'.

turns.line: Woman: Tell me about it! The bus is late too.
options: Yeah, it's always late when it's cold out.
Yeah, it always is late when is cold outside.
Yeah, he is always late when it cold out.
Yeah, it's always being late when it's cold out.
turns.answer: Yeah, it's always late when it's cold out.
turns.why: A bus is 'it', not 'he', and 'when' needs its own 'it's' to make a full sentence.

situation: You're at a friend's birthday party and meet someone new near the snacks.

We work together. I am starting at the company last year.
We work together. I start at the company last year.
We work together. I have started at the company last year.
turns.answer: We work together. I started at the company last year.
turns.why: Use the simple past with a finished time like 'last year'.

turns.line: Dana: Oh nice! Do you like it there?

Yeah, it's great. The people are really friend.
Yeah, it great. The peoples are really friendly.
Yeah, it's great. The people is really friendly.
turns.answer: Yeah, it's great. The people are really friendly.
turns.why: 'People' is already plural, so it takes 'are' and never gets an extra 's'.

turns.line: Dana: Good to hear. I'm getting a drink, do you want anything?

No, I don't want, thanks. Maybe later.
No, I'm not wanting, thanks. Maybe later.
No, thanks. I do not need, maybe later.
turns.answer: No, I'm good, thanks. Maybe later.
turns.why: 'I'm good' is the friendly, casual way to politely say no to an offer.

situation: You're in an elevator with a neighbor you don't know very well.

options: Pretty busy, but good. How about you?
Pretty busy, but good. And what about your things?
Pretty busy, but good. What is your news?
Pretty busy, but good. How are you been?
turns.answer: Pretty busy, but good. How about you?
turns.why: 'How about you?' is the simple, natural way to ask the same question back.

turns.line: Neighbor: Can't complain. Are you heading out for the day?

Just popping out for to grab some lunch.
Just pop out to take some lunch.
Just popping out for grabbing some lunch.
turns.answer: Just popping out to grab some lunch.
turns.why: Use 'to' plus a base verb to say why you're going somewhere.

situation: You're at a gym and the person on the next treadmill says hello.

turns.line: Guy: Hey, I haven't seen you here before. Are you new?
options: Yeah, I just joined last week.
Yeah, I just join last week.
Yeah, I have just joined last week.
Yeah, I am just joined last week.

turns.why: Use the simple past with 'last week'. Present perfect doesn't go with a finished time.

turns.line: Guy: Welcome! How are you finding it so far?
options: It's good, but I'm still getting used to it.
It's good, but I still get used to it.
It's good, but I'm still used to get it.
It's good, but I'm still getting use to it.
turns.answer: It's good, but I'm still getting used to it.
turns.why: 'Getting used to' means slowly becoming comfortable with something new, and it needs 'used', not 'use'.

situation: You're at a school event and chatting with another parent while kids play nearby.

turns.line: Parent: Your daughter is so energetic! How old is she?
options: She's seven. She never stops moving!
She has seven years. She never stops moving!
She is seven years old. She never stop moving!
She's having seven. She never stops moving!
turns.answer: She's seven. She never stops moving!
turns.why: In English we use 'is' for age, not 'has'. Hebrew speakers often say 'has years' by mistake.

turns.line: Parent: Ha, I know the feeling. Do you live around here?
options: Yeah, we live just a few minutes from here.
Yeah, we are living just few minutes of here.
Yeah, we live at a few minutes from here.
Yeah, we live just some minutes to here.
turns.answer: Yeah, we live just a few minutes from here.
turns.why: Say 'a few minutes from here', using 'from' and 'a few' for a small number.

turns.line: Parent: Oh, that's close! We should set up a playdate sometime.
options: That would be great! I'll give you my number.
That would be great! I'll give to you my number.
That would be great! I give you my number now.
That would be great! I will to give you number.
turns.answer: That would be great! I'll give you my number.
turns.why: Use 'will' for a spontaneous offer, and say 'give you', not 'give to you', before the thing.

situation: You're on a train and the person across from you notices your guidebook.

turns.line: Traveler: Are you visiting the city?
options: Yeah, it's my first time here. I'm here for a week.
Yeah, it's my first time here. I'm here since a week.
Yeah, it's my first time here. I'm here during a week.
Yeah, it's my first time here. I'm here a week ago.
turns.answer: Yeah, it's my first time here. I'm here for a week.
turns.why: Use 'for' to say how long something lasts, like 'for a week'.

turns.line: Traveler: Lovely! Have you planned what to see?

Not yet. Can you advise me some tips?
Not yet. You have any tip for me?
Not yet. Do you have some advices for me?
turns.answer: Not yet. Do you have any tips for me?
turns.why: 'Tips' can be counted, but 'advice' can't, so 'advices' is wrong. 'Do you have any' makes a natural question.

situation: You're at a barbecue at a friend's house, talking to another guest by the grill.

turns.line: Guest: This weather is perfect for a barbecue, right?

Totally. I hope it stay like this all afternoon.
Totally. I hope it staying like this all afternoon.
Totally. I hope it to stay like this all afternoon.
turns.answer: Totally. I hope it stays like this all afternoon.
turns.why: After 'I hope it', use the present tense with an 's': 'it stays'.

turns.line: Guest: Same! So, what do you do for work?
options: I'm a nurse. I work at a hospital downtown.
I'm nurse. I work in a hospital downtown.
I work as nurse. I work on a hospital downtown.
I'm a nurse. I'm working at hospital downtown.
turns.answer: I'm a nurse. I work at a hospital downtown.
turns.why: Jobs need 'a' (a nurse), and we say 'at a hospital' with the article before it.

turns.line: Guest: Wow, that must be tough. Do you like it?
options: I do, actually. It's tiring, but I love helping people.
I do, actually. It's tiring, but I love to help to people.
I do, actually. It's tired, but I love helping people.
I do, actually. It tires, but I love help people.
turns.answer: I do, actually. It's tiring, but I love helping people.
turns.why: Use 'tiring' for something that makes you tired. 'Tired' describes how you feel.

situation: You're at a language class break and a classmate asks about your plans.

turns.line: Classmate: Any plans for the weekend?

Not really. I might to go hiking if the weather is nice.
Not really. I maybe go hiking if the weather will be nice.
Not really. I might going hiking if weather is nice.
turns.answer: Not really. I might go hiking if the weather's nice.
turns.why: 'Might' is followed by the base verb with no 'to', and 'if' uses the present tense.

turns.line: Classmate: Sounds fun! Can I join you?

Sure, the more the merrier! I'll send you a message the details.
Sure, the more the merrier! I text you the details.
Sure, the more the merrier! I will texting you details.
turns.answer: Sure, the more the merrier! I'll text you the details.
turns.why: 'Text' works as a verb: 'text you the details'. Use 'I'll' for a quick decision.

situation: You're calling a dentist's office to book a check-up.

turns.line: Receptionist: Good morning, Bright Smile Dental. How can I help you?
options: Hi, I'd like to make an appointment for a check-up.
Hi, I want to do an appointment for a check-up.
Hi, I'd like to make a meeting for a check-up.
Hi, I want that you book me a check-up.
turns.answer: Hi, I'd like to make an appointment for a check-up.
turns.why: We 'make an appointment'. 'Do an appointment' and 'make a meeting' are word-for-word mistakes, and 'want that you' is wrong.
