Yes, please. I will to be there.
Yes, please. I am coming there already.
Yes, please. I'm being there.
turns.answer: Yes, please. I'll be there.
turns.why: "I'll be there" is the simple, natural way to promise you'll come. The other options mix up tense or word order.

turns.line: Receptionist: Perfect. Please arrive ten minutes early to fill out some forms.
options: Okay, no problem. See you then.
Okay, no problem. We will see us then.
Okay, no problem. I will meet you in that.
Okay, no problem. Until then see you.
turns.answer: Okay, no problem. See you then.
turns.why: "See you then" is a common, friendly way to end a call. The others are word-for-word translations.

situation: You're calling to cancel a gym trial class you booked for Saturday.

turns.line: Staff: FitZone, this is Chris speaking.
options: Hi Chris, I'm calling to cancel my class on Saturday.
Hi Chris, I call to cancel my class in Saturday.
Hi Chris, I am calling for cancelling my class Saturday.
Hi Chris, I want to cancel off my class on the Saturday.
turns.answer: Hi Chris, I'm calling to cancel my class on Saturday.
turns.why: "I'm calling to..." explains why you're calling. We use "on" with days of the week.

turns.line: Staff: No problem. Would you like to book a different day instead?
options: Maybe next week. Can I call you back about it?
Maybe next week. Can I call to you back about it?
Maybe next week. Can I return to you about it?
Maybe next week. I will be calling back to you.
turns.answer: Maybe next week. Can I call you back about it?
turns.why: "Call you back" is the usual phrase for calling again later. We don't say "call to you", and "return to you" is not used for phone calls.

situation: You're calling a bike repair shop to ask if your bike is ready.

turns.line: Mechanic: Hello, Pedal Power.
options: Hi, I dropped off my bike yesterday. Is it ready yet?
Hi, I leave my bike yesterday. It is ready already?
Hi, I was dropping my bike yesterday. Is it ready yet?
Hi, I have dropped off my bike yesterday. It's ready yet?
turns.answer: Hi, I dropped off my bike yesterday. Is it ready yet?
turns.why: Use the simple past with "yesterday". Use "yet" in questions about things you expect to be done.

turns.line: Mechanic: Almost. Can you pick it up around five?
options: Sure, I can be there by five.
Sure, I can to be there until five.
Sure, I am able to arrive on five.
Sure, I will be there at five about.
turns.answer: Sure, I can be there by five.
turns.why: "By five" means "at or before five". The other options use wrong words, wrong prepositions, or wrong word order.

turns.line: Mechanic: Great. Just bring the receipt with you.
options: Got it. Thanks a lot!
Got it. Thanks for all!
Got it. I thank you much!
Got it. Many thanks to you of this!
turns.answer: Got it. Thanks a lot!
turns.why: "Thanks a lot" is the normal, casual way to say thank you. The others are awkward translations.

situation: You're calling a language school to ask about an English course.

turns.line: Office: Good afternoon, Bright English. How can I help?
options: Hi, I'm interested in your evening course. Could you tell me more about it?
Hi, I interest in your evening course. Can you tell me more on it?
Hi, I'm interesting in your evening course. Could you say me more about it?
Hi, I want to know all of your evening course. Tell me more.
turns.answer: Hi, I'm interested in your evening course. Could you tell me more about it?
turns.why: We say "I'm interested in" (not "interesting"), and "tell me more about". The last option is too blunt.

turns.line: Office: Of course. The course starts on the 5th. Would you like to sign up?
options: Yes, could you send me the details by email?
Yes, can you send me the details on email?
Yes, send to me the details with the email.
Yes, I want you will send me details in mail.
turns.answer: Yes, could you send me the details by email?
turns.why: We send things "by email". The other options have wrong prepositions, word order, or sound too blunt.

situation: You're calling a customer service line, and the agent can't hear you clearly.

turns.line: Agent: Hello? I'm sorry, I can barely hear you. The line is bad.
options: Sorry, can you hear me now? Is that better?
Sorry, you hear me now? Is it more good?
Sorry, you can to hear me now? It is better?
Sorry, hear you me now? Is better like this?
turns.answer: Sorry, can you hear me now? Is that better?
turns.why: "Can you hear me now?" and "Is that better?" are what people say on a bad line. The others have wrong word order or grammar.

turns.line: Agent: Yes, that's better. How can I help you today?
options: I'm calling about my internet. It's been down since this morning.
I call about my internet. It is down from this morning.
I'm calling for my internet. It was down since this morning.
I am calling on my internet. It's down from the morning.
turns.answer: I'm calling about my internet. It's been down since this morning.
turns.why: Use "calling about" and the present perfect ("it's been down") with "since".

turns.line: Agent: I see. Let me check your account. Could you hold for a moment?
options: Sure, no rush. I'll hold.
Sure, no hurry. I am waiting you.
Sure, I will wait on the line to you.
Sure, take your time. I am staying here.
turns.answer: Sure, no rush. I'll hold.
turns.why: "I'll hold" is what people say on the phone when asked to wait. "Waiting you" is a wrong translation.

situation: You're calling a taxi company to get a ride to the airport tomorrow morning.

turns.line: Dispatcher: Yellow Cab, where would you like to go?
options: I need a taxi to the airport tomorrow at 6 a.m., please.
I need a taxi until the airport tomorrow on 6 a.m., please.
I want that a taxi will come to the airport tomorrow 6 a.m.
I need one taxi for to go to airport tomorrow in 6 a.m.
turns.answer: I need a taxi to the airport tomorrow at 6 a.m., please.
turns.why: We use "to" for a destination and "at" for a time. The other options have wrong prepositions and word order.

turns.line: Dispatcher: Okay. Can I have your address, please?
options: Sure. I'm at 12 Oak Street, near the park.
Sure. I live in 12 Oak Street, next the park.
Sure. My address is on 12 Oak Street, near to park.
Sure. I am staying at the 12 Oak Street, at the park near.
turns.answer: Sure. I'm at 12 Oak Street, near the park.
turns.why: "I'm at" plus the address is simple and natural. The others use wrong prepositions or awkward word order.

situation: You're at the office on Monday morning, talking to a coworker.

turns.line: Coworker: Hey, how was your weekend?
options: It was great, I went hiking with my brother.
It was great, I was going hiking with my brother.
It was great, I go hiking with my brother.
It was great, I am going hiking with my brother.
turns.answer: It was great, I went hiking with my brother.
turns.why: Use the past simple for finished events in the past, like last weekend.

turns.line: Coworker: Nice! Where did you go?
options: We went to a trail near the Sea of Galilee.
We went in a trail near the Sea of Galilee.
We were going to a trail near the Sea of Galilee.
We went at a trail near the Sea of Galilee.
turns.answer: We went to a trail near the Sea of Galilee.
turns.why: Use 'to' after 'go' when you talk about a place you travel to.

situation: You're in class and you didn't hear the teacher's last sentence.

turns.line: Teacher: Please open your books to page forty and start reading.
options: Sorry, could you say that again, please?
Sorry, what you said?
Sorry, I didn't hear you, say again.
Sorry, repeat me please.
turns.answer: Sorry, could you say that again, please?
turns.why: 'Could you say that again?' is the polite, natural way to ask someone to repeat.

turns.line: Teacher: Sure. Open your books to page forty.
options: Thanks, I'll start right now.
Thanks, I start right now.
Thanks, I'm starting since now.
Thanks, I will to start right now.
turns.answer: Thanks, I'll start right now.
turns.why: Use 'I'll' to say you decide to do something right now.

situation: You're in a meeting and your manager asks about a report you were working on.

turns.line: Manager: Hi Dana, is the sales report ready yet?
options: Almost. I just need to finish the last chart.
Almost. I need just finishing the last chart.
Almost. I just need finish the last chart.
Almost. I just needing to finish the last chart.
turns.answer: Almost. I just need to finish the last chart.
turns.why: 'Need' is followed by 'to' and the basic verb: need to finish.

turns.line: Manager: Great. When can you send it to me?
options: I'll send it to you by the end of the day.
I'll send it to you until the end of the day.
I'll send it to you in the end of the day.
I'll send it you to the end of the day.
turns.answer: I'll send it to you by the end of the day.
turns.why: 'By' means 'no later than' a certain time.

turns.line: Manager: Perfect. Thanks, Dana!
options: No problem. Let me know if you have any questions.
No problem. Let me to know if you have any questions.
No problem. Let me know if you will have any questions.
No problem. Say me if you have any questions.
turns.answer: No problem. Let me know if you have any questions.
turns.why: Use the present tense after 'if'. Say 'let me know', not 'let me to know' or 'say me'.

situation: You're a student talking to a classmate before an exam.

turns.line: Classmate: Are you ready for the exam tomorrow?
options: Not really. I haven't studied enough yet.
Not really. I didn't study enough until now.
Not really. I don't study enough yet.
Not really. I'm not studying enough yet.
turns.answer: Not really. I haven't studied enough yet.
turns.why: Use the present perfect with 'yet' for something that hasn't happened up to now.

turns.line: Classmate: Want to study together tonight?
options: Sure, that would really help. What time works for you?
Sure, that would really help. What time fits to you?
Sure, that would really help. In what hour you can?
Sure, that would really help. When is the time for you?
turns.answer: Sure, that would really help. What time works for you?
turns.why: 'What time works for you?' is the natural way to ask about a good time.

situation: You're calling in to work because you're not feeling well.

turns.line: Boss: Hi Tom, what's up? You sound terrible.
options: Yeah, I'm sick. I think I caught a cold.
Yeah, I'm sick. I think I took a cold.
Yeah, I'm sick. I think I got myself cold.
Yeah, I'm sick. I think I have caught cold of.
turns.answer: Yeah, I'm sick. I think I caught a cold.
turns.why: In English you 'catch' a cold. 'Take a cold' is a Hebrew-style mistake.

turns.line: Boss: Oh no. Do you want to take the day off?
options: Yes, if that's okay. I'll work from home tomorrow.
Yes, if that's okay. I'll work from home in tomorrow.
Yes, if that's okay. I working from home tomorrow.
Yes, if that's okay. I'll to work from home tomorrow.
turns.answer: Yes, if that's okay. I'll work from home tomorrow.
turns.why: Use 'I'll' plus the basic verb for a quick decision. No 'in' before 'tomorrow'.

turns.line: Boss: Sounds good. Get some rest!
options: Thanks, I will. Talk to you tomorrow.
Thanks, I will. I'll talk to you in tomorrow.
Thanks, I will. We talk tomorrow.
Thanks, I will. Talk to you the tomorrow.
turns.answer: Thanks, I will. Talk to you tomorrow.
turns.why: 'Talk to you tomorrow' is a natural goodbye. Don't add 'in' or 'the'.

situation: You're a new employee on your first day, meeting a teammate.

turns.line: Teammate: Hi, I'm Priya. Welcome to the team!
options: Thanks, Priya! It's nice to meet you.
Thanks, Priya! It's nice to know you.
Thanks, Priya! I'm pleasure to meet you.
Thanks, Priya! Nice to be meeting you.
turns.answer: Thanks, Priya! It's nice to meet you.
turns.why: Say 'nice to meet you' when you meet someone for the first time.

turns.line: Priya: So, what did you do before this job?
options: I worked at a small startup for three years.
I work at a small startup for three years.
I was working at a small startup since three years.
I have worked at a small startup before three years.
turns.answer: I worked at a small startup for three years.
turns.why: Use the past simple with 'for' for a finished period of time.

situation: You're in the school hallway and want to ask your teacher for more time on homework.

turns.line: Teacher: Hi Noa, did you need something?
options: Yes, could I get a few more days for the essay?
Yes, give me a few more days for the essay.
Yes, I want that you give me more days for the essay.
Yes, you need to give me more days for the essay.
turns.answer: Yes, could I get a few more days for the essay?
turns.why: 'Could I...?' is polite. The other options sound too blunt or rude to a teacher.

turns.line: Teacher: Hmm, why do you need more time?
options: I've been sick all week, so I'm a bit behind.
I'm sick all week, so I'm a bit behind.
I was sick since a week, so I'm a bit behind.
I'm being sick all week, so I'm a bit behind.
turns.answer: I've been sick all week, so I'm a bit behind.
turns.why: Use the present perfect for something that started in the past and continues until now.

turns.line: Teacher: Okay, you can hand it in on Friday.
options: Thank you so much! I really appreciate it.
Thank you so much! I really appreciate from you.
Thank you so much! I really am appreciating it.
Thank you so much! I really appreciate to you.
turns.answer: Thank you so much! I really appreciate it.
turns.why: 'Appreciate' needs an object like 'it'. No 'from' or 'to'.

situation: You're on a video call and the sound from your coworker keeps cutting out.

turns.line: Coworker: Can you hear me now?
options: Not really. You keep cutting out.
Not really. You are cutting out always.
Not really. You are keep cutting out.
Not really. You are being cut out.
turns.answer: Not really. You keep cutting out.
turns.why: 'Keep' plus '-ing' describes something that happens again and again.

turns.line: Coworker: Sorry about that. Let me try turning off my camera.
options: Good idea. That might help with the connection.
Good idea. That can maybe help to the connection.
Good idea. This is maybe helping the connection.
Good idea. That might helping with the connection.
turns.answer: Good idea. That might help with the connection.
turns.why: After 'might' use the basic verb: might help.

situation: You're at the office and want to borrow a charger from a coworker.

turns.line: Coworker: Hey Sam, you look stressed. Everything okay?
options: My phone is almost dead. Do you have a charger?
My phone is almost dying. Do you have charger?
My phone almost died. You have a charger for me?
My phone is almost dead. Are you having a charger?
turns.answer: My phone is almost dead. Do you have a charger?
turns.why: 'Almost dead' is common for a phone with no battery. Ask with 'Do you have a...?'

turns.line: Coworker: Yeah, I have one in my bag. What kind of phone do you have?
options: It's an old iPhone, so I need the Lightning one.
It's an old iPhone, so I need the Lightning that.
It's old iPhone, so I need the Lightning one.
It's an old iPhone, so I am needing the Lightning one.
turns.answer: It's an old iPhone, so I need the Lightning one.
turns.why: Use 'one' to avoid repeating 'charger'. 'Need' isn't normally used with '-ing'.

turns.line: Coworker: Oh, mine is USB-C. Sorry!
options: No worries. I'll ask someone else.
No worries. I ask someone else.
No worries. I'll ask to someone else.
No worries. I'm going ask someone else.
turns.answer: No worries. I'll ask someone else.
turns.why: 'Ask' doesn't need 'to'. Use 'I'll' for a quick decision.

situation: You're talking to a classmate about a group project you both have to finish.

turns.line: Classmate: We need to finish the presentation by Thursday. Can you do the slides?
options: Sure, I'll make the slides. Can you write the text?
Sure, I'll do the slides. Can you to write the text?
Sure, I make the slides. You can write the text?
Sure, I'll make the slides. Can you writing the text?
turns.answer: Sure, I'll make the slides. Can you write the text?
turns.why: Use 'I'll' for offering to do something, and 'can you' plus the basic verb to ask.

turns.line: Classmate: Okay. When should we meet to put it all together?
options: How about Wednesday after class?
How about Wednesday in after class?
How about Wednesday after of class?
What about to meet Wednesday after class?
turns.answer: How about Wednesday after class?
turns.why: 'How about...?' is a casual way to suggest a time. Don't add extra words like 'in', 'of' or 'to meet'.

turns.line: Classmate: Works for me. See you then!
options: Great, see you then!
Great, we see us then!
Great, see you in then!
Great, I see you then!
turns.answer: Great, see you then!
turns.why: 'See you then' is the short, natural way to say goodbye until a planned time.

situation: You're at the office on Monday morning, chatting with a coworker named Dana.

turns.line: Dana: Hey! How was your weekend?
options: It was great, thanks. I went hiking with my family.
It was great, thanks. I was going hiking with my family.
It was great, thanks. I go hiking with my family.
It was great, thanks. I have gone hiking with my family.
turns.answer: It was great, thanks. I went hiking with my family.
turns.why: Use the simple past for a finished event at a specific time, like last weekend.

turns.line: Dana: Nice! Did you get any work done, or did you totally switch off?
options: I totally switched off. I didn't even check my email.
I totally switched off. I didn't even to check my email.
I totally switched off. I even didn't check my email.
I totally switched off. I didn't even checked my email.
turns.answer: I totally switched off. I didn't even check my email.
turns.why: After "didn't", the verb stays in its base form: "check", not "checked".

situation: You're in a team meeting and your manager, Mr. Cole, is asking about a project.

turns.line: Mr. Cole: Where are we with the new website? Is it ready yet?
options: Almost. I just need to finish a couple of small things.
Almost. I need just finishing a couple of small things.
Almost. I just need finish a couple of small things.
Almost. I just need to finishing a couple of small things.
turns.answer: Almost. I just need to finish a couple of small things.
turns.why: "Need" is followed by "to" and the base verb: "need to finish".

turns.line: Mr. Cole: Okay. When can you send it to me?
options: I'll send it to you by the end of the day.
I send it to you until the end of the day.
I'll send it to you since the end of the day.
I'm sending it to you in the end of the day.
turns.answer: I'll send it to you by the end of the day.
turns.why: "By" means no later than a deadline. "Will" fits a quick promise made now.

turns.line: Mr. Cole: Perfect. Let me know if you run into any problems.
options: Will do. Thanks!
I will to do. Thanks!
Will to do. Thanks!
I do it. Thanks!
turns.answer: Will do. Thanks!
turns.why: "Will do" is the common casual way to say "I'll do that."

situation: You're at school and you ran into your classmate Noah in the hallway before class.

turns.line: Noah: Hey, did you do the homework for English?
options: Yeah, I finished it last night. Did you do it?
Yeah, I finish it last night. Did you do it?
Yeah, I have finished it yesterday night. Did you do it?
Yeah, I was finish it last night. Did you do it?
turns.answer: Yeah, I finished it last night. Did you do it?
turns.why: Use the simple past with a time word like "last night".

turns.line: Noah: Not yet. Can I copy yours quickly? Class starts in five minutes.
options: Sorry, I'd rather not. But I can help you do it.
Sorry, I'd rather not to. But I can help you do it.
Sorry, I don't want that you copy. But I can help you.
Sorry, I'd rather no. But I can help you doing it.
turns.answer: Sorry, I'd rather not. But I can help you do it.
turns.why: "I'd rather not" is a polite way to say no. After "help you", use the base verb.

situation: You're on a video call with a coworker named Priya, and your connection is bad.

turns.line: Priya: Sorry, you're breaking up. I can't hear you well.
options: Oh, sorry. I'll turn off my video. Is it better now?
Oh, sorry. I'll close my video. Is it better now?
Oh, sorry. I'll turn off my video. Is it more good now?
Oh, sorry. I'll turn off my video. Is better now?
turns.answer: Oh, sorry. I'll turn off my video. Is it better now?
turns.why: We "turn off" video, not "close" it. Questions need "is it" in that order.

turns.line: Priya: Yes, that's much better. So, can you share your screen?
options: Sure, give me a second. Can you see it now?
Sure, wait me a second. Can you see it now?
Sure, give me a second. Can you seeing it now?
Sure, give me a second. Do you can see it now?
turns.answer: Sure, give me a second. Can you see it now?
turns.why: "Give me a second" is natural. After "can", use the base verb, with no "do".

turns.line: Priya: Yep, I can see it. Go ahead.
options: Great. So, this is the report from last month.
Great. So, this is the report of the last month.
Great. So, this is the report from last month ago.
Great. So, that is the report from past month.
turns.answer: Great. So, this is the report from last month.
turns.why: We say "last month", with no "the" and no "ago".

situation: You're at a university cafeteria and a classmate named Liam sits down next to you.

turns.line: Liam: Hey! Are you ready for tomorrow's exam?
options: Not really. I've been studying all week, but I'm still nervous.
Not really. I study all week, but I'm still nervous.
Not really. I'm studying since a week, but I'm still nervous.
Not really. I was studying all week, but I still nervous.
turns.answer: Not really. I've been studying all week, but I'm still nervous.
turns.why: Use the present perfect continuous for something that started in the past and continues until now.

turns.line: Liam: Same here. Do you want to review the notes together after class?
options: Sure, that sounds good. Let's meet at the library.
Sure, that sounds good. Let's meeting at the library.
Sure, that sound good. Let's to meet at the library.
Sure, it sounds well. Let's meet in the library.
turns.answer: Sure, that sounds good. Let's meet at the library.
turns.why: After "let's", use the base verb. "Sounds good" is the natural phrase.

situation: You're at work and your coworker Tom just walked in looking tired.

turns.line: Tom: Ugh, I'm so tired. I barely slept last night.
options: Oh no. Why couldn't you sleep?
Oh no. Why you couldn't sleep?
Oh no. For what you couldn't sleep?
Oh no. Why didn't you could sleep?
turns.answer: Oh no. Why couldn't you sleep?
turns.why: In questions, the helper word comes before the subject: "couldn't you".

turns.line: Tom: My neighbors had a loud party. Anyway, do you have a minute? I need some advice.
options: Of course. What do you need?
Of course. What you need?
Of course. What are you needing?
Of course. What do you needing?
turns.answer: Of course. What do you need?
turns.why: Questions need "do" before the subject, and then the base verb: "What do you need?"

turns.line: Tom: I'm not sure how to tell my boss I need a day off next week.
options: Just ask her directly. I'm sure it'll be fine.
Just ask to her directly. I'm sure it'll be fine.
Just say her directly. I'm sure it'll be fine.
Just ask her direct. I'm sure it'll be fine.
turns.answer: Just ask her directly. I'm sure it'll be fine.
turns.why: "Ask" doesn't need "to" before the person, and "directly" is the adverb.

situation: You're calling a school office to ask about a parent-teacher meeting for your daughter.

turns.line: Secretary: Good afternoon, Oak Hill School. How can I help you?
options: Hi, I'd like to schedule a meeting with my daughter's teacher, please.
Hi, I want that you make me a meeting with my daughter's teacher.
Hi, I'd like to schedule a meeting to my daughter's teacher, please.
Hi, I want to set a meeting to my daughter's teacher, please.
turns.answer: Hi, I'd like to schedule a meeting with my daughter's teacher, please.
turns.why: "I'd like to" is polite, and we schedule a meeting "with" someone.

turns.line: Secretary: Of course. Does Thursday at 4 o'clock work for you?
options: Thursday is a bit hard for me. Do you have anything on Friday?
Thursday is not good for me. Have you something on Friday?
Thursday doesn't suit to me. Is there something on Friday?
Thursday is a bit hard for me. You have anything on Friday?
turns.answer: Thursday is a bit hard for me. Do you have anything on Friday?
turns.why: Questions with "have" need "do you have" in this everyday use.

situation: You're at your first day at a new job, and a coworker named Sarah is showing you around.

turns.line: Sarah: And this is the kitchen. Help yourself to coffee anytime.
options: Thanks! That's really nice of you.
Thanks! That's very nice from you.
Thanks! This is really nice by you.
Thanks! It's really nice to you.
turns.answer: Thanks! That's really nice of you.
turns.why: We say "nice of you" to thank someone for being kind.

turns.line: Sarah: By the way, we usually have lunch together around noon. Want to join?
options: I'd love to! Where do you usually go?
I'd love! Where do you usually going?
I love to! Where you usually go?
I'd love to! Where are you usually go?
turns.answer: I'd love to! Where do you usually go?
turns.why: "I'd love to" accepts an invitation, and questions about habits use "do you".

turns.line: Sarah: There's a place around the corner. They have great sandwiches.
options: Sounds great. I'm starving, so I'm in!
Sounds great. I'm very hunger, so I'm in!
Sounds great. I have hunger, so I'm in!
Sounds great. I'm starving, so I'm in it!
turns.answer: Sounds great. I'm starving, so I'm in!
turns.why: "I'm starving" means very hungry, and "I'm in" means "count me in".

situation: You're in a hallway at school and you want to ask your teacher, Ms. Reed, for more time on a project.

turns.line: Ms. Reed: Hi! Did you need something?
options: Yes, could I have a few more days to finish my project?
Yes, could I having a few more days to finish my project?
Yes, could I to have a few more days to finish my project?
Yes, can you extending my deadline for my project?
turns.answer: Yes, could I have a few more days to finish my project?
turns.why: After "could I", use the base verb: "could I have...?"

turns.line: Ms. Reed: Hmm, why do you need more time?
options: I've had a lot of tests this month, so I'm a bit behind.
I had a lot of tests this month, so I'm behind a bit from.
I have a lot of tests since this month, so I'm a bit behind.
I'm having a lot of tests this month, so I'm behind of it.
turns.answer: I've had a lot of tests this month, so I'm a bit behind.
turns.why: Use the present perfect for a period of time that includes now, like "this month".

turns.line: Ms. Reed: I understand. You can hand it in on Monday.
options: Thank you so much. I really appreciate it.
Thank you so much. I really appreciate.
Thank you so much. I really appreciate to you.
Thank you so much. I'm really appreciating it.
turns.answer: Thank you so much. I really appreciate it.
turns.why: "Appreciate" always needs an object, like "it".

situation: You're at a coffee machine at work and a coworker named Jake asks about your plans for the day.

turns.line: Jake: Hey, what are you working on today?
options: I'm preparing a presentation for tomorrow's meeting.
I prepare a presentation for tomorrow's meeting.
I'm preparing a presentation to tomorrow's meeting.
I'm prepare a presentation for tomorrow's meeting.
turns.answer: I'm preparing a presentation for tomorrow's meeting.
turns.why: Use the present continuous for what you're doing today or right now.

turns.line: Jake: Cool. Do you want some help with the slides?
options: That would be great, thanks. I'm running out of time.
That would be great, thanks. I'm finishing from time.
That would be great, thanks. I don't have time enough.
That would be great, thanks. My time is going out.
turns.answer: That would be great, thanks. I'm running out of time.
turns.why: "Running out of time" is the natural way to say you have almost no time left.

situation: You're at the office on Monday morning and a coworker greets you.

turns.line: Coworker: Hey Dana, how was your weekend?
options: It was great, we went hiking near the lake. And yours?
It was great, we were going hiking near the lake. And yours?
It was great, we go hiking near the lake. And yours?
It was great, we have gone hiking near the lake. And yours?
turns.answer: It was great, we went hiking near the lake. And yours?
turns.why: Use the simple past for a finished event at a specific time, like last weekend.

turns.line: Coworker: Nice! Mine was quiet. I mostly stayed home and watched shows.
options: Sounds relaxing. Sometimes you just need a slow weekend.
Sounds relaxing. Sometimes you just needs a slow weekend.
Sounds relaxing. Sometimes it's needed to you a slow weekend.
Sounds relaxing. Sometimes you are needing a slow weekend.
turns.answer: Sounds relaxing. Sometimes you just need a slow weekend.
turns.why: "Need" is a state verb, so we use the simple present, not the -ing form. With "you" it's "need", not "needs".

situation: You're a student and you didn't understand something your teacher just explained.

turns.line: Teacher: Okay, that's the end of the lesson. Any questions before we finish?
options: Yes, could you explain the last part again, please?
Yes, you can explain me the last part again, please?
Yes, explain the last part again, please, now.
Yes, could you to explain the last part again, please?
turns.answer: Yes, could you explain the last part again, please?
turns.why: "Could you + verb" is a polite request. Don't add "to" after "could you".

turns.line: Teacher: Sure. Which part wasn't clear?
options: The part about how to write the conclusion.
The part about how write the conclusion.
The part about how to write for the conclusion.
The part about how to the conclusion write.
turns.answer: The part about how to write the conclusion.
turns.why: "How to" is followed by a verb, and then the object comes after it.

turns.line: Teacher: Got it. A conclusion should just sum up your main points. Does that help?
options: Yes, that makes sense now. Thanks a lot!
Yes, that makes me sense now. Thanks a lot!
Yes, that is making sense now. Thanks a lot!
Yes, that has sense now. Thanks a lot!
turns.answer: Yes, that makes sense now. Thanks a lot!
turns.why: "Make sense" is the normal phrase for "I understand it now."

situation: You're in a meeting and your manager asks about a report you were working on.

turns.line: Manager: Hi Omar, is the sales report ready yet?
options: Almost. I'll send it to you by the end of the day.
Almost. I send it to you until the end of the day.
Almost. I'll send you it on the end of the day.
Almost. I'm going send it to you by end of day.
turns.answer: Almost. I'll send it to you by the end of the day.
turns.why: Use "by" for a deadline, and "I'll" for a quick decision or promise.

turns.line: Manager: Great. Can you also add last month's numbers?
options: Sure, no problem. I'll add them now.
Sure, no problem. I add them now.
Sure, no problem. I will to add them now.
Sure, no problem. I'm adding them from now.
turns.answer: Sure, no problem. I'll add them now.
turns.why: "I'll" is the natural way to agree to do something right away.

situation: You're a student and you bump into a classmate in the hallway before an exam.

turns.line: Classmate: Hey Noa! Are you ready for the math test?
options: Not really. I didn't study enough.
Not really. I didn't studied enough.
Not really. I haven't studied enough yesterday.
Not really. I don't studied enough.
turns.answer: Not really. I didn't study enough.
turns.why: After "didn't" we use the base verb: "study", not "studied".

turns.line: Classmate: Same here. Want to look at the notes together for a few minutes?
options: Yes, good idea. Let's do it.
Yes, good idea. Let's to do it.
Yes, good idea. Let us doing it.
Yes, good idea. We let do it.
turns.answer: Yes, good idea. Let's do it.
turns.why: "Let's" is followed directly by the base verb, with no "to" or -ing.

situation: You're calling your boss early in the morning because you feel sick.

turns.line: Boss: Hello, this is Mark.
options: Hi Mark, it's Yael. I'm not feeling well today.
Hi Mark, here is Yael. I'm not feeling well today.
Hi Mark, I am Yael. I don't feel myself well today.
Hi Mark, it's Yael. I'm feeling badly today.
turns.answer: Hi Mark, it's Yael. I'm not feeling well today.
turns.why: On the phone we say "it's + name", not "here is" or "I am".

turns.line: Boss: Oh no, sorry to hear that. Will you be able to come in later?
options: I don't think so. I'm going to stay home and rest.
I don't think so. I'm going to stay in home and rest.
I don't think so. I'm going stay at the home and rest.
I don't think so. I stay home and rest.
turns.answer: I don't think so. I'm going to stay home and rest.
turns.why: We say "stay home" (not "in home" or "at the home"), and "going to" shows a plan.

turns.line: Boss: Okay, take care. Let me know if you need anything.
options: Thanks, I appreciate it. I'll keep you updated.
Thanks, I appreciate. I'll keep you update.
Thanks, I appreciate it. I keep you updated.
Thanks, I appreciate it. I'll keep updating you for it.
turns.answer: Thanks, I appreciate it. I'll keep you updated.
turns.why: "Appreciate" needs "it", and "keep you updated" means you'll share news later.

situation: You're a new employee talking to a coworker in the kitchen on your first week.

turns.line: Coworker: Hi! You must be the new guy. I'm Ben.
options: Yes, I started on Monday. Nice to meet you, Ben.
Yes, I start since Monday. Nice to meet you, Ben.
Yes, I'm starting from Monday. Nice to meet you, Ben.
Yes, I have started in Monday. Nice to meet you, Ben.
turns.answer: Yes, I started on Monday. Nice to meet you, Ben.
turns.why: Use the simple past and "on" with a day of the week.

turns.line: Coworker: Welcome! How are you finding it so far?
options: It's great. Everyone has been really friendly.
It's great. Everyone are really friendly.
It's great. All the people has been really friendly.
It's great. Everyone is being really friendly since.
turns.answer: It's great. Everyone has been really friendly.
turns.why: "Everyone" is singular, and present perfect fits something that started in the past and continues.

situation: You're in class and the teacher is handing back homework, but yours is missing.

turns.line: Teacher: Here's your homework, Liam. Oh wait, I don't see yours. Did you hand it in?
options: I think so. I put it on your desk on Tuesday.
I think so. I put it in your desk in Tuesday.
I think so. I have put it on your desk yesterday.
I think so. I was putting it on your desk on Tuesday.
turns.answer: I think so. I put it on your desk on Tuesday.
turns.why: Use "on" for a desk and for a day, and the simple past for a finished action.

turns.line: Teacher: Hmm, I can't find it. Could you bring it again tomorrow?
options: Of course. I'll bring another copy tomorrow.
Of course. I bring another copy tomorrow.
Of course. I'll bring another copy to tomorrow.
Of course. I will to bring another copy tomorrow.
turns.answer: Of course. I'll bring another copy tomorrow.
turns.why: "I'll" is the natural way to promise something, and we don't use "to" before "tomorrow".

situation: You're chatting with a coworker at lunch about a busy week.

turns.line: Coworker: You look tired, Sara. Is everything okay?
options: Yeah, I've been working late all week.
Yeah, I work late all the week.
Yeah, I'm working late since a week.
Yeah, I was working late all week until now.
turns.answer: Yeah, I've been working late all week.
turns.why: Use the present perfect continuous for something that started in the past and is still going.

turns.line: Coworker: Ouch. When is your deadline?
options: It's due this Friday, so I'm almost done.
It's due in this Friday, so I'm almost done.
It due this Friday, so I almost done.
It's due on this Friday, so I'm almost finished it.
turns.answer: It's due this Friday, so I'm almost done.
turns.why: We say "this Friday" with no preposition, and "I'm almost done" needs the verb "am".

turns.line: Coworker: Well, good luck. Let me know if I can help.
options: Thanks, I will. I'll take a real break after Friday.
Thanks, I will. I take a real break after Friday.
Thanks, I will. I'll make a real break after Friday.
Thanks, I will. I'll do a real break after Friday.
turns.answer: Thanks, I will. I'll take a real break after Friday.
turns.why: We say "take a break", not "make" or "do" a break.

situation: You're a student asking your teacher about an assignment after class.

turns.line: Teacher: Hi Tomer. Did you need something?
options: Yes, I wanted to ask when the essay is due.
Yes, I wanted to ask when is the essay due.
Yes, I wanted to ask when the essay it is due.
Yes, I wanted to ask for when the essay is due.
turns.answer: Yes, I wanted to ask when the essay is due.
turns.why: In an indirect question the word order stays normal: "when the essay is due".

turns.line: Teacher: It's due next Wednesday.
options: Okay, thanks. Can I send it by email?
Okay, thanks. Can I send it in the email?
Okay, thanks. Can I send it with email?
Okay, thanks. Can I send it on email?
turns.answer: Okay, thanks. Can I send it by email?
turns.why: We say "by email" to describe the way we send something.

turns.line: Teacher: Yes, that's fine. Just make sure it's a PDF.
options: No problem. I'll make sure it is.
No problem. I'll be sure it is.
No problem. I make sure it is.
No problem. I'll make sure that is.
turns.answer: No problem. I'll make sure it is.
turns.why: "Make sure it is" is the natural phrase, and "I'll" shows you agree to do it.

situation: You're in a team meeting and your colleague asks if you can cover for them.

turns.line: Colleague: Hey Tom, I have a dentist appointment on Thursday. Could you cover for me in the meeting?
options: Sure, what time does the meeting start?
Sure, what time the meeting starts?
Sure, in what hour starts the meeting?
Sure, when is starting the meeting?
turns.answer: Sure, what time does the meeting start?
turns.why: Questions need "does" before the subject, and then the base verb "start".

turns.line: Colleague: It's at ten. You just need to give a quick update on the project.
options: Okay, that's easy. I'll prepare something tonight.
Okay, that's easy. I'll prepare something in the night.
Okay, that's easy. I prepare something tonight.
Okay, that's easy. I'll prepare me something tonight.
turns.answer: Okay, that's easy. I'll prepare something tonight.
turns.why: We say "tonight" with no preposition, and "I'll" is natural for a quick decision.

situation: You're a student working on a group project, and a teammate is late with their part.

turns.line: Teammate: Hey Lena, sorry, I haven't finished my slides yet.
options: No worries. When do you think you'll be done?
No worries. When you think you will finish?
No worries. When do you think you will to be done?
No worries. Until when you think you're done?
turns.answer: No worries. When do you think you'll be done?
turns.why: Questions with "think" use "do you think" first, then normal word order.

turns.line: Teammate: Probably by tonight. I'm really sorry about that.
options: That's fine. Just send them to me when they're ready.
That's fine. Just send to me them when they're ready.
That's fine. Just send them to me when they will be ready.
That's fine. Just send them for me when they ready.
turns.answer: That's fine. Just send them to me when they're ready.
turns.why: After "when" we use the present tense even for the future, so "they're ready", not "will be".

turns.line: Teammate: Will do. Thanks for being so understanding!
options: Anytime. We're a team, so we help each other.
Anytime. We are a team, so we are helping us.
Anytime. We're a team, so we help one to other.
Anytime. We a team, so we help each other.
turns.answer: Anytime. We're a team, so we help each other.
turns.why: "Each other" is the natural way to say people do something for one another.

situation: You're at a coffee shop and your laptop battery is almost dead.

turns.line: Barista: Hi there! What can I get for you?
options: Could I get a latte, please? Also, is there a free plug nearby?
I want a latte. And where I can to charge my laptop?
Give me a latte. Is there a place for put my laptop?
I take a latte. You have maybe some electric for me?
turns.answer: Could I get a latte, please? Also, is there a free plug nearby?
turns.why: "Could I get..." is polite, and "is there a free plug nearby?" is a natural way to ask.

turns.line: Barista: Sure, there's one by the window. It's a bit loose, though.
options: Thanks! If it doesn't work, I'll come back and ask you.
Thanks! If it will not work, I come back and ask you.
Thanks! If it doesn't works, I will to come back to you.
Thanks! When it not working, I am coming back to ask.
turns.answer: Thanks! If it doesn't work, I'll come back and ask you.
turns.why: After "if", use the present tense ("doesn't work"). Use "will" only for the result ("I'll come back").

situation: You're at a hotel and the Wi-Fi in your room isn't working.

turns.line: Receptionist: Good evening, how can I help you?
options: Hi, the Wi-Fi in my room isn't working. Could you take a look?
Hi, the Wi-Fi in my room not works. You can to fix it?
Hi, in my room the Wi-Fi doesn't working. Fix it now.
Hi, I have a problem with Wi-Fi in the room, do something.
turns.answer: Hi, the Wi-Fi in my room isn't working. Could you take a look?
turns.why: It states the problem clearly and asks politely with "Could you...?"

turns.line: Receptionist: I'm so sorry about that. Have you tried reconnecting?
options: Yes, I tried that twice, but it still doesn't connect.
Yes, I try that two times, but it still not connect.
Yes, I was trying it twice, but it doesn't connecting.
Yes, I have tried that before two times but it no connects.
turns.answer: Yes, I tried that twice, but it still doesn't connect.
turns.why: Use the simple past ("tried") for something you did already, and "twice" for two times.

turns.line: Receptionist: Okay, I'll send someone up in ten minutes.
options: That would be great, thanks. I really appreciate it.
That will be great, thanks. I appreciate to you it.
It's okay for me, thanks. I am appreciating this.
Good, thanks. I will be appreciate if he comes quickly.
turns.answer: That would be great, thanks. I really appreciate it.
turns.why: "That would be great" is a friendly, natural reply, and "I appreciate it" says thank you well.

situation: You're in a restaurant and your soup has arrived cold.

turns.line: Waiter: How is everything so far?
options: Sorry to bother you, but my soup is a bit cold.
Sorry to bother you, but my soup is a bit of cold.
Sorry for bother you, but the soup is cold like ice.
Sorry to bother you, but my soup it is too much cold.
turns.answer: Sorry to bother you, but my soup is a bit cold.
turns.why: It's polite and simple. "A bit cold" sounds gentle, not angry.

turns.line: Waiter: Oh no, I'm sorry! Would you like me to heat it up or bring a new one?
options: Could you heat it up, please? That would be great.
You can heat it up, please? That will be great to me.
Heat it up, please. This is great for me, okay.
Could you to heat it up, please? It's great by me.
turns.answer: Could you heat it up, please? That would be great.
turns.why: After "Could you", use the basic verb ("heat") with no "to".

situation: You're at the airport and you can't find your gate.

turns.line: Staff member: Can I help you with something?
options: Yes, please. I'm looking for Gate 24. Do you know where it is?
Yes, please. I search Gate 24. You know where is it?
Yes, please. I look for Gate 24. Where it is located?
Yes, please. I am looking Gate 24. Do you know where is?
turns.answer: Yes, please. I'm looking for Gate 24. Do you know where it is?
turns.why: Say "looking for" and keep normal word order after "where": "where it is".

turns.line: Staff member: It's down this hall, on your left. About a five-minute walk.
options: Sorry, I didn't catch that. Could you say it again?
Sorry, I didn't catch that. You can say it again?
Sorry, I didn't catch that. Repeat this one more time.
Sorry, I didn't caught that. Could you say it again?
turns.answer: Sorry, I didn't catch that. Could you say it again?
turns.why: "I didn't catch that" means you didn't hear it. "Could you say it again?" politely asks someone to repeat.

turns.line: Staff member: Sure. Down the hall and turn left. You can't miss it.
options: Got it, thank you so much for your help!
Got it, thank you so much for the help to me!
Understood, thank you very much of your help!
Got it, thanks a lot on your help!
turns.answer: Got it, thank you so much for your help!
turns.why: We say "thank you for" something. "Got it" is a casual way to say you understand.

situation: You're in a shop and the shirt you bought has a hole in it.

turns.line: Cashier: Hi, what can I do for you?
options: Hi, I bought this shirt yesterday and it has a hole in it.
Hi, I buy this shirt yesterday and it has a hole inside.
Hi, I have bought this shirt yesterday and there is hole.
Hi, yesterday I am buying this shirt and it has hole on it.
turns.answer: Hi, I bought this shirt yesterday and it has a hole in it.
turns.why: Use the simple past ("bought") with "yesterday". "A hole in it" is the natural phrase.

turns.line: Cashier: Oh, I'm sorry about that. Do you have the receipt?
options: Yes, here you go. Can I exchange it for a new one?
Yes, here you go. I can to change it with a new?
Yes, take it. Can I replace it on another one?
Yes, here it is. You can exchange me it for new?
turns.answer: Yes, here you go. Can I exchange it for a new one?
turns.why: We "exchange something for" another thing. "Here you go" is what we say when handing something over.

situation: You're on a train and someone is sitting in the seat you reserved.

turns.line: Stranger: Oh, is this your seat?
options: I think so. I reserved seat 12A. Could you check your ticket?
I think so. I have reserved seat 12A. You check your ticket.
I think yes. I ordered the seat 12A. Look at your ticket.
I think so. I reserve seat 12A. Can you to see your ticket?
turns.answer: I think so. I reserved seat 12A. Could you check your ticket?
turns.why: It's polite and clear. "Reserved" is the right past form, and "Could you check...?" is gentle.

turns.line: Stranger: Oh, you're right, mine is 12B. Sorry about that!
options: No worries, it happens! Thanks for moving.
No worries, it happen! Thanks for the moving.
Not a problem, it is happening! Thank you to move.
No worry, it happens to me! Thanks that you moved.
turns.answer: No worries, it happens! Thanks for moving.
turns.why: "No worries" is a friendly, casual reply, and "thanks for" is followed by the -ing form.

situation: You're at work and your neighbor in the open office is playing loud music.

turns.line: Colleague: Hey, did you need something?
options: Sorry, would you mind turning the music down a little?
Sorry, you can to turn down the music a little?
Sorry, turn the music down because it bothers to me.
Sorry, would you mind to turn down the music little?
turns.answer: Sorry, would you mind turning the music down a little?
turns.why: After "would you mind", use the -ing form. It's a polite way to ask.

turns.line: Colleague: Oh, I'm so sorry! I didn't realize it was that loud.
options: No problem. I'm trying to focus on a report, that's all.
No problem. I try to focus on a report, that is all.
No problem. I'm trying focus on one report, that's it.
No problem. I was try to focus about a report, that's all.
turns.answer: No problem. I'm trying to focus on a report, that's all.
turns.why: Use the present continuous ("I'm trying") for something happening right now, and "focus on" for the topic.

turns.line: Colleague: Got it. I'll put my headphones on.
options: Thanks, I really appreciate that. Have a good day!
Thanks, I really appreciate it that. Have good day!
Thanks, I am really appreciating. Have a nice day to you!
Thanks, I really appreciate that. Have the good day!
turns.answer: Thanks, I really appreciate that. Have a good day!
turns.why: "I appreciate that" is a natural thank-you, and we say "Have a good day" with "a".

situation: You're at a gym and the treadmill you're using suddenly stops working.

turns.line: Trainer: Hey, is everything okay over here?
options: Not really. This treadmill just stopped working. Can you help?
Not really. This treadmill is stopping to work. You help me?
Not really. This treadmill just stopped to working. Help me.
Not really. The treadmill didn't works now. Can you to help?
turns.answer: Not really. This treadmill just stopped working. Can you help?
turns.why: "Stopped working" is the natural phrase for something that breaks. "Just" shows it happened a moment ago.

turns.line: Trainer: Let me take a look. Hmm, it might be unplugged.
options: Oh, I didn't think of that! Is it okay if I use another one?
Oh, I didn't thought about that! It's okay I use other one?
Oh, I not think of that! Can I to use another one?
Oh, I didn't think about it that! Is okay if I use another?
turns.answer: Oh, I didn't think of that! Is it okay if I use another one?
turns.why: After "didn't", use the basic verb ("think"). "Is it okay if I...?" is a polite request.

situation: You're calling customer service because your internet keeps cutting out.

turns.line: Agent: Thanks for calling. How can I help you today?
options: Hi, my internet keeps cutting out, and it's really frustrating.
Hi, my internet is cutting out all the time, it frustrates.
Hi, my internet keep cut out, and I am very frustrating.
Hi, my internet cuts out every time, and I'm frustrating about it.
turns.answer: Hi, my internet keeps cutting out, and it's really frustrating.
turns.why: "Keeps" plus the -ing form shows something that happens again and again. "It's frustrating" describes the problem.

turns.line: Agent: I'm sorry to hear that. How long has this been happening?
options: It's been happening for about a week now.
It happens since about one week now.
It is happening from a week already.
It has happened since a week ago now.
turns.answer: It's been happening for about a week now.
turns.why: Use the present perfect ("has been happening") with "for" and a length of time.

turns.line: Agent: Thanks. I can send a technician tomorrow morning.
options: That works for me. Could you make it after nine, please?
That works for me. Can you do it after nine, please me?
This is working for me. Could you to make after nine?
That is okay with me. Make it after the nine, please.
turns.answer: That works for me. Could you make it after nine, please?
turns.why: "That works for me" is a natural way to agree. "Could you...?" keeps the request polite.

situation: You're in a taxi and the driver is going the wrong way.

turns.line: Driver: Almost there. Just a few more minutes.
options: Sorry, I think we missed the turn. Could you check the map?
Sorry, I think we are missing the turn. You check the map?
Sorry, I think we miss the turn. Check the map, please me.
Sorry, I think we missed the turn. Could you to check map?
turns.answer: Sorry, I think we missed the turn. Could you check the map?
turns.why: "Missed" is the past form for a turn already passed. "Could you check...?" is polite and direct.

turns.line: Driver: Oh, you're right. Let me turn around at the next street.
options: Thanks. I have a meeting at two, so I'm a bit short on time.
Thanks. I have a meeting on two, so I am little short with time.
Thanks. I have meeting in two, so I'm a bit short in the time.
Thanks. I had a meeting at two, so I'm short from time a bit.
turns.answer: Thanks. I have a meeting at two, so I'm a bit short on time.
turns.why: We say "at two" for a clock time and "short on time" for not having much of it.

situation: You're at a restaurant and your pasta has just arrived, but it's cold.

turns.line: Waiter: Hi there! How's everything tasting so far?
options: Sorry to bother you, but my pasta is a bit cold.
Sorry to bother you, but my pasta is cold a little.
Sorry to bother you, but my pasta are a bit cold.
Hey, my pasta is cold. Take it back and fix it.
turns.answer: Sorry to bother you, but my pasta is a bit cold.
turns.why: It's polite, 'a bit' softens the complaint, and the grammar is correct. The others have wrong word order, wrong 'are', or sound rude.

turns.line: Waiter: Oh, I'm so sorry! Would you like me to heat it up, or bring you a new one?
options: A new one would be great, thanks.
I want that you will bring me a new one.
Bring a new one. And hurry up, I'm hungry.
A new one would be great, thanks you.
turns.answer: A new one would be great, thanks.
turns.why: 'Would be great, thanks' is a friendly, natural way to choose. 'I want that you will' is a word-for-word Hebrew pattern.

situation: You're at a hotel and the air conditioning in your room isn't working.

turns.line: Receptionist: Front desk, how can I help you?
options: Hi, the air conditioning in my room isn't working.
Hi, the air conditioning in my room not working.
Hi, the air conditioning in my room doesn't work since morning.
Hi, fix the air conditioning in my room right now.
turns.answer: Hi, the air conditioning in my room isn't working.
turns.why: Use 'isn't working' for a problem happening now. 'Not working' needs 'is', and 'since morning' needs a different tense.

turns.line: Receptionist: I'm sorry about that. I'll send someone up in about ten minutes.
options: Great, thanks. Could you also send up some water?
Great, thanks. I want also that you send water.
Great, thanks. You must also send me some water.
Great, thanks. Could you also send up some waters?
turns.answer: Great, thanks. Could you also send up some water?
turns.why: 'Could you also...' is a polite request. 'Water' is not counted, so 'waters' is wrong, and 'you must' is too bossy.

situation: You're at a train station and you can't work out the ticket machine.

turns.line: Woman: You look a bit lost. Do you need a hand?
options: Yes, please. I can't figure out this ticket machine.
Yes, please. I can't to figure out this ticket machine.
Yes, please. I don't know how it works this machine.
Yes. Just do it for me, I don't have time for this.
turns.answer: Yes, please. I can't figure out this ticket machine.
turns.why: 'Can't figure out' is a natural way to say you don't understand something. After 'can't' we don't use 'to'.

turns.line: Woman: Sure. Where are you trying to go?
options: I'm trying to get to Brighton, but the screen froze.
I try to get to Brighton, but the screen froze.
I'm trying to arrive to Brighton, but the screen froze.
I'm trying to get in Brighton, but the screen froze.
turns.answer: I'm trying to get to Brighton, but the screen froze.
turns.why: Use present continuous for what you're doing right now, and 'get to' a place. 'Arrive to' and 'get in' are wrong here.

turns.line: Woman: Ah, it does that sometimes. Just tap the screen twice.
options: It worked, thank you so much! I owe you one.
It worked, thank you so much! I owe to you one.
It worked, thank you so much! I'm owing you one.
It worked, thank you so much! I'm in debt for you.
turns.answer: It worked, thank you so much! I owe you one.
turns.why: 'I owe you one' is a friendly phrase after a favor. 'Owe' has no 'to' here and isn't used in the continuous.

situation: Your neighbor's music has been loud late at night, so you knock on their door.

turns.line: Neighbor: Oh, hi! Is everything okay?
options: Hi! Sorry to bug you, but could you turn the music down a bit?
Hi! Sorry to bug you, but you must turn the music down now.
Hi! Sorry to bug you, but could you close the music down a bit?
Hi! Sorry to bug you, but could you to turn the music down?
turns.answer: Hi! Sorry to bug you, but could you turn the music down a bit?
turns.why: 'Could you turn it down' is a polite request. 'Close the music' is from Hebrew, and 'you must' is too harsh.

turns.line: Neighbor: Oh no, I'm so sorry. I didn't realize it was that loud.
options: No worries, I just have an early start tomorrow.
No worries, I just have early start tomorrow.
No worries, I just have an early start since tomorrow.
It's your fault, I have an early start tomorrow.
turns.answer: No worries, I just have an early start tomorrow.
turns.why: 'No worries' keeps things friendly, and 'an early start' needs 'an'. 'Since' is for the past, not the future.

situation: You call customer service because the online order you received is wrong.

turns.line: Agent: Thanks for calling Shopzone, this is Dana. How can I help?
options: Hi, I ordered a blue jacket, but I got a red one.
Hi, I have ordered a blue jacket yesterday, but I got a red one.
Hi, I ordered a blue jacket, but it came me a red one.
Hi, you sent me the wrong jacket. What is wrong with you?
turns.answer: Hi, I ordered a blue jacket, but I got a red one.
turns.why: Use past simple for finished actions. 'Have ordered' doesn't go with 'yesterday', and 'it came me' is wrong.

turns.line: Agent: I'm sorry about that. Can I have your order number?
options: Sure, it's 4471. Could you send me the right one?
Sure, it's 4471. Send me the right one immediately.
Sure, it's 4471. Could you send to me the right one?
Sure, it's 4471. Could you sent me the right one?
turns.answer: Sure, it's 4471. Could you send me the right one?
turns.why: After 'could you' we use the basic verb 'send'. 'Send me' has no 'to', and a polite request beats an order.

turns.line: Agent: Of course. We'll send the right one today and email you a return label.
options: Perfect, thanks for sorting this out so fast.
Perfect, thanks for sort this out so fast.
Perfect, thanks that you sorted this out fast.
Perfect, finally. It should have been right the first time.
turns.answer: Perfect, thanks for sorting this out so fast.
turns.why: After 'thanks for' we use the -ing form. 'Thanks that you' is a Hebrew-style pattern, and the last option sounds annoyed.

situation: You're at the office and the printer has jammed again.

turns.line: Tom: Hey, you look stressed. What's up?
options: The printer's jammed again. Do you know how to fix it?
The printer's jammed again. Do you know to fix it?
The printer's jammed again. Do you know how fixing it?
The printer's jammed again. Fix it, you're good with this stuff.
turns.answer: The printer's jammed again. Do you know how to fix it?
turns.why: We say 'know how to' plus a basic verb. Telling a colleague to fix it is too pushy.

turns.line: Tom: Yeah, you just have to open the back panel. Want me to show you?
options: That'd be great, thanks. I'd really appreciate it.
That'd be great, thanks. I would appreciate to you.
That'd be great, thanks. I'm really appreciating it.
No, just do it for me. I'm busy with other things.
turns.answer: That'd be great, thanks. I'd really appreciate it.
turns.why: 'I'd really appreciate it' is a warm way to accept help. 'Appreciate' isn't used with 'to you' or in the continuous.

situation: You've been waiting a long time for your coffee at a café.

turns.line: Barista: Hi there, can I help you?
options: Hi, I ordered a latte about twenty minutes ago.
Hi, I order a latte since twenty minutes.
Hi, I'm ordering a latte before twenty minutes.
Hi, where's my latte? Twenty minutes is too much!
turns.answer: Hi, I ordered a latte about twenty minutes ago.
turns.why: Use past simple with 'ago' for a finished action. 'Since' and 'before' are the wrong words for this.

turns.line: Barista: Oh, let me check. What name was the order under?
options: It's under Maya. I don't think it's been made yet.
It's on Maya. I don't think it was made yet.
It's under Maya. I think nobody is making it still.
It's under Maya. You probably forgot about it, right?
turns.answer: It's under Maya. I don't think it's been made yet.
turns.why: We say an order is 'under' a name, and 'it's been made yet' uses present perfect with 'yet'. Blaming the barista sounds rude.

turns.line: Barista: You're right, sorry! I'll make it right now, and it's on the house.
options: Oh, that's really kind of you. Thank you!
Oh, that's really kind from you. Thank you!
Oh, that's really kind of you. Thanks you!
Oh, finally. Next time just make it faster.
turns.answer: Oh, that's really kind of you. Thank you!
turns.why: 'Kind of you' is the fixed phrase, and 'thank you' needs no extra 's'. The last option is rude after an apology.

situation: You're in an English class and you didn't hear what the teacher just said.

turns.line: Teacher: Okay, everyone, please do exercise four for homework.
options: Sorry, could you say that again? I didn't catch it.
Sorry, could you say that again? I didn't catched it.
Sorry, you could say it again? I didn't catch.
Sorry, what? Say it again, I wasn't listening.
turns.answer: Sorry, could you say that again? I didn't catch it.
turns.why: 'Could you say that again?' is polite, and 'didn't catch it' means you didn't hear. After 'didn't' use 'catch'.

turns.line: Teacher: Sure! Exercise four, page twelve. It's due on Thursday.
options: Thanks. I'm also stuck on question three. Could you explain it?
Thanks. I'm also stuck on question three. Could you explain me it?
Thanks. I also stuck on question three. Could you explain it?
Thanks. I'm also stuck on question three. You must explain it.
turns.answer: Thanks. I'm also stuck on question three. Could you explain it?
turns.why: We need 'am' in 'I'm stuck', and 'explain it' has no 'me'. Politeness matters when asking a teacher.

situation: You're at the airport and your suitcase didn't show up after the flight.

turns.line: Agent: Baggage services. How can I help you?
options: Hi, my suitcase didn't come out on the belt.
Hi, my suitcase didn't came out on the belt.
Hi, my suitcase not exit from the belt.
Hi, you lost my suitcase! This is unacceptable!
turns.answer: Hi, my suitcase didn't come out on the belt.
turns.why: After 'didn't' we use the basic verb 'come'. The last option attacks the agent instead of asking for help.

turns.line: Agent: I'm sorry to hear that. Can you describe it for me?
options: Sure, it's a small black one with a red tag.
Sure, it's a black small one with a red tag.
Sure, it's small black one with red tag.
Sure, it is a small black what has a red tag.
turns.answer: Sure, it's a small black one with a red tag.
turns.why: Size comes before color in English, and we need 'a' before 'small' and 'red tag'.

turns.line: Agent: Thanks. We'll track it down and deliver it to your hotel tomorrow.
options: Okay, thanks. Could you call me as soon as you know?
Okay, thanks. Could you call me as soon as you will know?
Okay, thanks. Could you to call me as soon as you know?
Okay. Call me the second you know, I'm not waiting.
turns.answer: Okay, thanks. Could you call me as soon as you know?
turns.why: After 'as soon as' we use present simple, not 'will'. After 'could you' we don't use 'to'.

situation: Your car is in the garage and you need a ride tomorrow, so you call a friend.

turns.line: Noa: Hey! What's up? You sound stressed.
options: My car's in the shop. Any chance you could give me a ride tomorrow?
My car's in the shop. Any chance you can to give me a ride tomorrow?
My car's in the shop. Any chance you could drive me a ride tomorrow?
My car's in the shop. You will give me a ride tomorrow, okay?
turns.answer: My car's in the shop. Any chance you could give me a ride tomorrow?
turns.why: 'Any chance you could...' is a soft, friendly way to ask a favor. We 'give' a ride, not 'drive' one.

turns.line: Noa: Sure, where to? I'm free after two.
options: To the airport. I'll pay for gas, of course.
To the airport. I'll pay you the gas, of course.
To the airport. I'll paid for gas, of course.
To the airport. You'll pay for gas, of course.
turns.answer: To the airport. I'll pay for gas, of course.
turns.why: 'Pay for' gas is the natural phrase, and 'I'll' plus the basic verb offers to pay. Wrong tense or wrong person breaks the meaning.

situation: You're at a café and your coffee has gone cold.

turns.line: Waiter: Hi there, is everything okay with your drink?
options: Actually, it's a bit cold. Could you heat it up, please?
Actually, it is a bit cold. You must to heat it up now.
Actually, it's a bit cold. Why you didn't heat it up?
Actually, my coffee is cold. I want that you heat it.
turns.answer: Actually, it's a bit cold. Could you heat it up, please?
turns.why: "Could you..." with "please" is a polite way to ask for a fix. The other options are rude or use the wrong grammar.

turns.line: Waiter: Here you go, nice and hot. Sorry about that! Anything else I can get you?
options: No, that's all. Thanks for sorting it out.
No, that's all. Thanks for you sort it out.
No, that's all. Thanks for sorting out it.
No, that's all. Thank you for to sort it.
turns.answer: No, that's all. Thanks for sorting it out.
turns.why: After "thanks for" we use the -ing form, and "it" goes in the middle: "sorting it out".

situation: You're in a hotel room and the air conditioning isn't working.

turns.line: Receptionist: Front desk, how can I help you?
options: Hi, the air conditioning in room 305 isn't working.
Hi, the air conditioning in room 305 doesn't works.
Hi, the air conditioning in room 305 not work now.
Hi, you must fix the air conditioning in room 305.
turns.answer: Hi, the air conditioning in room 305 isn't working.
turns.why: "Isn't working" describes a problem happening right now. It's clear and polite, not an order.

turns.line: Receptionist: I'm sorry about that. I can send someone up in about twenty minutes.
options: That would be great, thank you. I'll wait in the room.
That would be great, thank you. I'll waiting in the room.
That would be great, thank you. I'm wait at the room.
That would be great, thank you. I'll wait on the room.
turns.answer: That would be great, thank you. I'll wait in the room.
turns.why: We say "I'll wait" for a decision made now, and "in the room" for being inside.

turns.line: Receptionist: Would you like us to move you to a different room instead?
options: No, thanks. I'd rather stay if it gets fixed quickly.
No, thanks. I'd rather to stay if it gets fixed quickly.
No, thanks. I'd rather stayed if it gets fixed quickly.
No, thanks. I prefer rather stay if it get fixed quickly.
turns.answer: No, thanks. I'd rather stay if it gets fixed quickly.
turns.why: "I'd rather" is followed by the plain verb, with no "to": "I'd rather stay".

situation: You're at a train station and the ticket machine is confusing you.

turns.line: Stranger: You look a bit lost. Need a hand?
options: Yes, please. I can't work out how this machine works.
Yes, please. I can't understand how works this machine.
Yes, please. I don't know how to working this machine.
Yes, please. I can't to figure how it works this.
turns.answer: Yes, please. I can't work out how this machine works.
turns.why: "Work out" means figure out. In a question word clause, the order stays normal: "how this machine works".

turns.line: Stranger: Just press here, then choose your destination.
options: Got it. And where do I tap my card?
Got it. And where I tap my card?
Got it. And where do I tapping my card?
Got it. And where I do tap my card?
turns.answer: Got it. And where do I tap my card?
turns.why: In a question we say "where do I..." with the plain verb: "where do I tap".

situation: Your neighbor is playing loud music late at night, so you knock on their door.

turns.line: Neighbor: Oh, hi. Is something wrong?
options: Sorry to bother you, but the music is quite loud. Could you turn it down?
Sorry to bother you, but the music is very loud. Turn it down right now.
Sorry to disturb you, but the music is loud. Can you to turn it down?
Sorry to bother you, but the music is loud. Could you turn down it?
turns.answer: Sorry to bother you, but the music is quite loud. Could you turn it down?
turns.why: Starting with "sorry to bother you" and asking "Could you...?" is polite. With "it", we say "turn it down".

turns.line: Neighbor: Oh no, I had no idea. I'll turn it down now.
options: Thanks, I really appreciate it. Have a good night!
Thanks, I really appreciate. Have a good night!
Thanks, I'm really appreciating it. Have a good night!
Thanks, I really appreciate to you. Have a good night!
turns.answer: Thanks, I really appreciate it. Have a good night!
turns.why: "Appreciate" needs an object, so we say "I appreciate it". Here we don't use the -ing form.

situation: You're at a restaurant and the waiter brings you chicken instead of the pasta you ordered.

turns.line: Waiter: Here you go, enjoy your meal!
options: Excuse me, I think there's been a mistake. I ordered the pasta.
Excuse me, I think there was a mistake. I am ordering the pasta.
Excuse me, I think there's been a mistake. I was order the pasta.
Excuse me, I think there's a mistake. I order the pasta before.
turns.answer: Excuse me, I think there's been a mistake. I ordered the pasta.
turns.why: "I think there's been a mistake" is a gentle way to complain. "Ordered" is the past tense for something already done.

turns.line: Waiter: Oh, I'm so sorry! Should I bring the pasta, or would you like to keep the chicken?
options: The pasta, please. I don't mind waiting a few minutes.
The pasta, please. I don't mind to wait a few minutes.
The pasta, please. I don't mind wait a few minutes.
The pasta, please. I not mind waiting a few minutes.
turns.answer: The pasta, please. I don't mind waiting a few minutes.
turns.why: After "mind" we use the -ing form: "I don't mind waiting".

turns.line: Waiter: It'll be about ten minutes. I'll also bring you a free drink.
options: That's very kind of you, thank you.
That's very kind from you, thank you.
That's very kindly of you, thank you.
That's very kind for you, thank you.
turns.answer: That's very kind of you, thank you.
turns.why: The fixed phrase is "kind of you". It's a polite way to thank someone for a nice gesture.

situation: Your internet has been down for two days, so you call customer support.

turns.line: Agent: Thanks for calling. How can I help you today?
options: Hi, my internet has been down since Monday. Can you help me?
Hi, my internet is down since Monday. Can you help me?
Hi, my internet was down since Monday. Can you help me?
Hi, my internet doesn't work from Monday. Can you help me?
turns.answer: Hi, my internet has been down since Monday. Can you help me?
turns.why: For a problem that started in the past and is still going, we use the present perfect with "since".

turns.line: Agent: I'm sorry to hear that. Can I have your account number?
options: Sure, it's 4471. How long will it take to fix?
Sure, it's 4471. How much time it will take to fix?
Sure, it's 4471. How long it takes to fix it?
Sure, it's 4471. How long will it take fixing?
turns.answer: Sure, it's 4471. How long will it take to fix?
turns.why: "How long will it take to..." is the natural question about time. The verb after "to" stays plain.

turns.line: Agent: A technician can come tomorrow between 9 and 12.
options: Tomorrow morning works for me. Could you send me a confirmation?
Tomorrow morning works to me. Could you send me a confirmation?
Tomorrow morning works for me. Can you sends me a confirmation?
Tomorrow morning works for me. Could you send to me confirmation?
turns.answer: Tomorrow morning works for me. Could you send me a confirmation?
turns.why: We say "works for me" about a time. "Send me a confirmation" is the natural word order.

situation: You're at the gym and you can't figure out how to adjust a machine.

turns.line: Trainer: Hey! Everything alright over there?

Not really. Could you show me how adjust this seat?
Not really. Could you to show me how I adjust this seat?
Not really. You show me how to adjust this seat.
turns.answer: Not really. Could you show me how to adjust this seat?
turns.why: "Could you show me how to..." is a polite request for help. We say "how to" plus the plain verb.

turns.line: Trainer: Sure! Pull the lever and slide the seat up or down.
options: Oh, I see. Is that high enough, or should I go lower?
Oh, I see. Is that enough high, or should I go lower?
Oh, I see. This is high enough, or I should go lower?
Oh, I see. Is that high enough, or should I going lower?
turns.answer: Oh, I see. Is that high enough, or should I go lower?
turns.why: "Enough" comes after the adjective: "high enough". After "should I" we use the plain verb.

situation: You're at work and the printer jams just before an important meeting.

turns.line: Colleague: You look stressed. What's going on?
options: The printer's jammed and my meeting starts in ten minutes.
The printer is jam and my meeting starts in ten minutes.
The printer's jammed and my meeting starts after ten minutes.
The printer's jammed and my meeting will to start in ten minutes.
turns.answer: The printer's jammed and my meeting starts in ten minutes.
turns.why: "Jammed" describes the printer's state, and "in ten minutes" means ten minutes from now.

turns.line: Colleague: Ugh, that's annoying. I'm going up to the second floor, and the printer there works.
options: Oh, great! Would you mind printing these for me?
Oh, great! Would you mind to print these for me?
Oh, great! Would you mind printing these to me?
Oh, great! Do you mind that you print these for me?
turns.answer: Oh, great! Would you mind printing these for me?
turns.why: After "would you mind" we use the -ing form, and we say "for me" when someone does something to help us.

situation: You bought headphones yesterday, but one side doesn't work, so you go back to the shop.

turns.line: Clerk: Welcome back! What can I do for you?

I buy these yesterday, but the left side doesn't work.
I bought these yesterday, but the left side doesn't works.
I have bought these yesterday, but the left side doesn't work.
turns.answer: I bought these yesterday, but the left side doesn't work.
turns.why: "Yesterday" needs the simple past: "bought". After "doesn't" the verb stays plain: "work".

turns.line: Clerk: Sorry about that. Do you have the receipt?
options: Yes, here it is. Can I get a refund or an exchange?
Yes, here it is. Can I take a refund or a change?
Yes, here is it. Can I get a refund or an exchange?
Yes, here it is. Can I to get a refund or exchange?
turns.answer: Yes, here it is. Can I get a refund or an exchange?
turns.why: We say "get a refund" and "an exchange". "Here it is" keeps this word order.

situation: You're a student and you need more time to finish an essay, so you talk to your teacher.

turns.line: Teacher: Hi, did you want to see me?
options: Yes, I was wondering if I could have a bit more time for the essay.
Yes, I was wondering if I could to have a bit more time for the essay.
Yes, I was wondering that I could have a bit more time at the essay.
Yes, I was wondering if I can had a bit more time for the essay.
turns.answer: Yes, I was wondering if I could have a bit more time for the essay.
turns.why: "I was wondering if I could..." is a very polite way to ask. After "could" we use the plain verb.

turns.line: Teacher: I see. What's the problem?
options: I've been sick all week, so I couldn't finish it.
I'm sick all week, so I couldn't finish it.
I have sick all week, so I couldn't finish it.
I've been sick all week, so I can't finished it.
turns.answer: I've been sick all week, so I couldn't finish it.
turns.why: For something that started in the past and lasted until now, we use the present perfect: "I've been sick".

turns.line: Teacher: Okay, you can hand it in on Friday.
options: Thank you so much. I'll make sure it's on your desk by Friday.
Thank you so much. I'll make sure it be on your desk until Friday.
Thank you so much. I'll make sure it's on your desk since Friday.
Thank you so much. I'll make sure it will on your desk by Friday.
turns.answer: Thank you so much. I'll make sure it's on your desk by Friday.
turns.why: After "make sure" we use the present simple: "it's". "By Friday" means no later than Friday. "Until" is for something that keeps going up to a time.
